objectives: Starting from the two-neuron recurrent equation, compute by hand the eigenvalues, normalized eigenvectors, and input coordinates of the common and difference modes.
Use each mode's time constant to classify stable decay, leaky integration, perfect integration, and unstable growth, then reinterpret the mode coordinates as trajectories in neural activity space.
Derive PCA by maximizing the projection variance of centered data, and work through numerical examples of top-K projection, reconstruction, variance explained, and dimensional truncation.

Distinguish rigorously between dynamical modes of a recurrent weight matrix and principal components of a covariance matrix, including when they may align and when no such alignment should be expected.
Compare eigenvalue-cliff, cumulative-variance, and held-out-performance criteria for choosing dimensionality.
prerequisiteBridge: Begin by viewing a vector as an ordered list of numbers. At one moment, the firing-rate deviations of two neurons can be written \(h=(h_{1},h_{2})^\mathrm{T}\); matrix W specifies the feedback each neuron receives from the other. If \(Wv=\lambda v\), one recurrent mapping simply multiplies activity along v by \(\lambda\), making v a natural direction for describing the network. The only matrix skills required are a two-by-two determinant, simultaneous linear equations, vector length, and dot products.

The dynamical equation \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\) contains intrinsic leak, recurrent feedback, and external input. Expanding h in the eigenvector basis of W separates the coupled system into independent one-dimensional equations. For \(\tau  d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha +\beta\), removing the input leaves exponential decay with effective time constant \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\). Decay slows as \(\lambda\) approaches 1; at \(\lambda =1\), this linear mode retains its accumulated state.

PCA answers a different question. Given population vectors from many times or trials, it finds a unit direction v that maximizes the variance of the centered projection \(v^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\). PCA uses the data covariance C, not W itself. Always ask whether a matrix comes from a model or from data before interpreting its eigenvectors; this prevents dynamical modes, principal components, and causal circuit directions from being conflated.

diagnostic.prompt: What is the result of multiplying \(W=[[0,0.6],[0.6,0]]\) by \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\)?
diagnostic.answer: The result is \((0.6,0.6)^\mathrm{T}\), so \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.6.
diagnostic.explanation: Multiply row by row: the first row gives \(0\times 1+0.6\times 1\) and the second gives \(0.6\times 1+0\times 1\). If this calculation is unfamiliar, return to the common/difference-mode module and check each component.

diagnostic.prompt: For \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(\lambda =0.8\), what is the effective time constant of \(\tau  d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha\)?
diagnostic.answer: \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.8)=100 \mathrm{ms}\).
diagnostic.explanation: The coefficient \(1-\lambda\) sets the decay rate: the smaller this gap, the longer the time constant. Do not mistake \(\lambda\) itself for a time constant measured in milliseconds.

diagnostic.prompt: Why must each neuron's mean activity be subtracted before computing the covariance?
diagnostic.answer: Centering makes covariance describe joint fluctuations around the mean firing pattern instead of mistaking the mean response direction for the direction of greatest variability.
diagnostic.explanation: Without centering, the second moment h \(h^\mathrm{T}\) contains both the mean outer product and trial-to-trial variation, so PC1 may primarily track mean activity.

diagnostic.prompt: Does a nearly one-dimensional trajectory mean that only one neuron is active?
diagnostic.answer: No. It means that the joint activity of many neurons varies mainly along one population direction, which usually contains nonzero components from multiple neurons.
diagnostic.explanation: Dimension counts independent, variable population coordinates; it does not count nonzero neurons. Return to the activity-space reconstruction to see how both neurons participate in the common mode.

diagnostic.prompt: If the PCA eigenvalues are 9, 3, 1, and 1, what cumulative variance is explained by retaining the first two PCs?
diagnostic.explanation: The denominator of cumulative variance explained must contain every eigenvalue. Dividing only by the retained eigenvalues would incorrectly give 100%.

modules.title: Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does replacing h1 and h2 with common and opposing changes decouple the originally coupled network?
paragraphs: The source page gives \(W=[[0,w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\) and the rate equations \(\tau  dh_{1}/dt=-h_{1}+w_{0}h_{2}+I_{1}\) and \(\tau  dh_{2}/dt=-h_{2}+w_{0}h_{1}+I_{2}\). Zeros on the diagonal mean that this teaching example has no self-coupling, while equal off-diagonal entries make the reciprocal coupling symmetric. That symmetry suggests testing \(h_{1}=h_{2}\) and \(h_{1}=-h_{2}\): exchanging the neurons leaves the first pattern unchanged and changes only the sign of the second.

Set \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}-w_{0}^{2}=0\) to obtain \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) and \(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{+}\) gives \(h_{2}=h_{1}\), so a common eigenvector is \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{-}\) gives \(h_{2}=-h_{1}\), so a difference eigenvector is \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Dividing each by \(\sqrt 2\) produces unit vectors with zero dot product, an orthonormal basis V. Normalization preserves direction and lets coordinates be computed directly by dot products.

The new coordinates are \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\): \(\alpha _{+}=(h_{1}+h_{2})/\sqrt 2\) and \(\alpha _{-}=(h_{1}-h_{2})/\sqrt 2\). Applying the same transformation to the input gives \(\beta _{+}=(I_{1}+I_{2})/\sqrt 2\) and \(\beta _{-}=(I_{1}-I_{2})/\sqrt 2\). Substitute \(h=V\alpha\) into the original equation and left-multiply by \(V^\mathrm{T}\) to obtain \(\tau  d\alpha _{+}/dt=-(1-w_{0})\alpha _{+}+\beta _{+}\) and \(\tau  d\alpha _{-}/dt=-(1+w_{0})\alpha _{-}+\beta _{-}\). Each equation now contains only its own coordinate, confirming that the basis change has decoupled the dynamics.

Both modes are population patterns, not patterns belonging separately to neuron 1 and neuron 2. Increasing the common mode changes both neurons in the same direction; increasing the difference mode raises one and lowers the other. In an asymmetric network the eigenvectors need not be orthogonal, so \(V^{-1}\) need not equal \(V^\mathrm{T}\). Mode decomposition may still be possible, but the coordinate transform and geometry must use the general inverse rather than the orthogonal formulas on this page.
keyPoints: \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\).
\(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized difference vector \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\).
Activity and input must be transformed in the same basis: \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T}h\) and \(\beta =V^\mathrm{T}I\).
The eigenvectors of W describe directions of model dynamics; they are not the PCs obtained from data covariance.

derivation.title: Complete solution of the common/difference eigensystem
derivation.setup: Start from \(Wv=\lambda v\) and \(\det(W-\lambda I)=0\) without guessing the answer, then normalize the two eigenvectors and assemble V.

steps.title: Write the characteristic equation
steps.explanation: For \(W-\lambda I=[[-\lambda ,w_{0}],[w_{0},-\lambda ]]\), the two-by-two determinant is \((-\lambda )(-\lambda )-w_{0}^{2}\).

steps.title: Solve for the two directions
steps.explanation: When \(\lambda =w_{0}\), both rows require \(v_{1}=v_{2}\); when \(\lambda =-w_{0}\), they require \(v_{1}=-v_{2}\). Choose the shortest integer vector in each direction and then normalize it.

steps.title: Construct the coordinate transform
steps.explanation: Place the eigenvectors in the columns of V. Because they are orthogonal unit vectors, \(V^{-1}=V^\mathrm{T}\).

steps.title: Transform the dynamics
steps.explanation: Use \(V^\mathrm{T}WV=\operatorname{diag}(w_{0},-w_{0})\) to split the original coupled system into two scalar equations.

symbolNotes: h, I, \(\alpha\), and \(\beta\) are \(2\times 1\) vectors; W and V are \(2\times 2\) matrices.
w0 and the eigenvalues are dimensionless feedback gains; \(\tau\) carries the unit of time.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(V^\mathrm{T}h\) has shape \((2\times 2)(2\times 1)=2\times 1\), and every term in the mode ODE has units of a rate coordinate.
derivation.limitCheck: At \(w_{0}=0\) the original neurons are uncoupled and the two basis directions decay at the same rate. The eigenbasis is then not unique: common/difference coordinates remain valid but are no longer the only choice.

workedExample.title: Transform a population state into mode coordinates
workedExample.problem: Given \(h=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(I=(2,2)^\mathrm{T}\), calculate \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), then verify that \(\alpha\) reconstructs h without loss.
steps: Compute \(\alpha _{+}=(3+1)/\sqrt 2=2\sqrt 2\) and \(\alpha _{-}=(3-1)/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\).
Compute \(\beta _{+}=(2+2)/\sqrt 2=2\sqrt 2\) and \(\beta _{-}=(2-2)/\sqrt 2=0\), so the input drives only the common mode.
Reconstruct \(\alpha +\xi _{+}+\alpha -\xi _{-}\): the first component is \((2\sqrt 2+\sqrt 2)/\sqrt 2=3\) and the second is \((2\sqrt 2-\sqrt 2)/\sqrt 2=1\).
workedExample.result: The mode coordinates are \(\alpha =(2\sqrt 2,\sqrt 2)^\mathrm{T}\), the input coordinates are \(\beta =(2\sqrt 2,0)^\mathrm{T}\), and reconstruction returns exactly \((3,1)^\mathrm{T}\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: The squared coordinates sum to \(8+2=10\), matching the original vector's squared length \(3^{2}+1^{2}=10\). An orthogonal transform preserves length, providing an arithmetic check.

selfCheck.prompt: If \(I_{1}=1\) and \(I_{2}=-1\), which mode is driven directly?
selfCheck.answer: \(\beta _{+}=(1-1)/\sqrt 2=0\) and \(\beta _{-}=(1-(-1))/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\), so only the difference mode is driven directly; the neurons tend to change in opposite directions.

pitfalls: Omitting \(1/\sqrt 2\) makes the coordinate and reconstruction scales inconsistent.
Treating the common and difference modes as separate neurons, even though each mode is a joint pattern of both neurons.

modules.title: Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does the same w0 slow the common mode but accelerate the difference mode?
paragraphs: The homogeneous mode equations are \(\tau  d\alpha _{+}/dt=-(1-w_{0})\alpha _{+}\) and \(\tau  d\alpha _{-}/dt=-(1+w_{0})\alpha _{-}\). Comparing them with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}} d\alpha /dt=-\alpha\) gives \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1-w_{0})\) and \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1+w_{0})\). Page 1 of the source writes \(1/(1\mp w_{0})\), which is valid only after normalizing \(\tau\) to 1; otherwise it loses the time unit. The dimensionally complete expression is \(\tau /(1\mp w_{0})\). Positive coupling supplies positive feedback to common changes and cancels part of the intrinsic leak. For opposing changes it acts as restoring feedback, because a rise in neuron 1 drives neuron 2 upward and reduces their difference.

When \(|w_{0}|<1\), both 1-w0 and 1+w0 are positive, so both modes decay exponentially after input removal. As w0 approaches 1, \(\tau _{+}\) becomes long and the common coordinate behaves as a leaky integrator. At \(w_{0}=1\) the common equation has no leak: sustained input is integrated and the accumulated \(\alpha _{+}\) remains after the input ends. The same logic moves to the difference mode as w0 approaches -1. Equality marks a perfect integrator and should not be lumped into the ordinary leaky regime.

If \(|w_{0}|>1\), at least one coefficient becomes negative. For example, at \(w_{0}=1.2\) the common equation is \(\tau  d\alpha _{+}/dt=+0.2\alpha _{+}\), so a small perturbation grows exponentially. Mathematical instability does not \(\operatorname{mean} a\) real firing rate can increase without bound; neuronal saturation, thresholds, and inhibition change the large-amplitude behavior. Linear analysis nevertheless identifies a direction that leaves the fixed point locally.

Read the activity-space sketches as follows. In the h1-h2 plane, the common axis has slope +1 and the difference axis has slope -1. If \(\tau _{-}\) is much smaller than \(\tau _{+}\), an arbitrary initial state rapidly loses its difference component, approaches the common axis, and then moves slowly along it. The drawn axes show eigenvector directions; trajectory speed comes from the eigenvalues and \(\tau\), not from the lengths of the lines.
keyPoints: \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1-w_{0})\) and \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1+w_{0})\); the signs cannot be collapsed into a common denominator.
Only \(|w_{0}|<1\) makes both modes stable; \(w_{0}=\pm 1\) produces a perfect integrator in one mode.
\(|w_{0}|>1\) makes the linear fixed point unstable along at least one mode.
An activity-space trajectory decomposes into independent exponential components along the eigenvectors.

derivation.title: Read the effective time constant from the mode coefficient
derivation.setup: Rewrite each mode as a standard first-order relaxation equation, then classify the coefficient's sign in each parameter range.

steps.title: Isolate the standard decay rate
steps.explanation: Rewrite \(\tau  d\alpha _{+}/dt=-(1-w_{0})\alpha _{+}\) as \(d\alpha _{+}/dt=-[(1-w_{0})/\tau ]\alpha _{+}\).

steps.title: Invert the rate to obtain the time constant
steps.explanation: The exponential decay rate is \((1-w_{0})/\tau\), so its reciprocal is the time constant; the difference mode follows identically.

steps.title: Classify the boundary
steps.explanation: A positive denominator gives decay, zero gives retention or integration, and a negative denominator gives exponential growth.

steps.title: Add constant input
steps.explanation: Under stable conditions, setting the derivative to zero gives \(\alpha _{+}*=\beta _{+}/(1-w_{0})\), showing that gain also rises near the critical point.

symbolNotes: \(\alpha \pm\) and \(\beta \pm\) are rate coordinates. If the original input is a current, first determine whether I has already been converted to rate drive in the model.
\(\tau \pm\) has units of time, whereas w0 and \(1\pm w_{0}\) are dimensionless.
derivation.unitsCheck: Because the denominator is dimensionless, \(\tau /(1\mp w_{0})\) retains the time unit of \(\tau\). A unitless 'time constant' signals that \(\tau\) was omitted.
derivation.limitCheck: As w0→1^-, \(\tau +\to \infty\). Beyond 1 the formula becomes negative; this is not a negative physical time but a sign that the exponent now describes growth.

workedExample.title: Compare the speeds of the two modes
workedExample.problem: Let the single-cell time constant be \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(w_{0}=0.8\). Remove the input, calculate both mode time constants, and predict the fraction remaining after 100 ms.
steps: After 100 ms, the common-mode amplitude fraction is \(e^{-100/100}=e^{-1}\approx 0.368\).
The difference-mode fraction is \(e^{-100/11.11}=e^{-9}\approx 0.000123\), so it has nearly vanished.
workedExample.result: At 100 ms the state contains almost only the common component, although both neurons may still have nonzero activity.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Setting w0 to 0 should return both time constants to 20 ms. One long and one short time constant here agrees with the direction of positive reciprocal feedback.

selfCheck.prompt: At \(w_{0}=-0.9\), which mode is slowest, and what is its time constant in units of \(\tau\)?
selfCheck.answer: The difference mode is slowest because \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1-0.9)=10\tau\); the common mode has \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1+0.9)\approx 0.526\tau\). Negative coupling near -1 preserves the opposing-change pattern.

pitfalls: Judging stability from the sign of an eigenvalue of W while forgetting the -h term in the full ODE.
Using \(\tau /(1-w_{0})\) for both modes and thereby losing the negative sign of the difference eigenvalue.

modules.title: Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory
modules.guidingQuestion: Precisely what does 'nearly one-dimensional population dynamics' mean, and what does it not claim?
paragraphs: Activity space uses (h1,h2) to describe the state of both neurons at each moment; mode space uses \((\alpha _{+},\alpha _{-})\) to describe the same point. An invertible V connects the two, so they are not distinct datasets. Activity space corresponds directly to recorded firing rates, whereas mode space exposes the dynamics because each \(\alpha\) coordinate evolves with its own time constant. A coordinate change removes no information; dimensionality reduction occurs only when coordinates are later discarded.

Any state can be written \(h(t)=\alpha +(t)\xi _{+}+\alpha -(t)\xi _{-}\). If \(\tau _{-}\) is much smaller than \(\tau _{+}\) and no persistent difference input acts during the delay, \(\alpha -(t)\) decays much faster than \(\alpha +(t)\). After several \(\tau _{-}\), \(h(t)\approx \alpha +(t)\xi _{+}\) and subsequent states lie near the common axis. 'One-dimensional' means that \(\alpha _{+}\) is the main free coordinate needed for the trajectory, not that only one neuron participates.

Approximation quality can be measured by residual energy. Because the basis is orthonormal, \(||h||^{2}=\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2}\). Discarding the difference mode gives squared reconstruction error exactly \(\alpha -^{2}\). An analyst may set a tolerance, for example calling the state 95% common-mode when \(\alpha -^{2}/(\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2})<0.05\). This criterion is chosen for the analysis; it is not an absolute boundary that appears automatically in a sketch.

This reasoning also states the conditions for a low-dimensional conclusion. Strong drive to \(\beta - at\) every moment or trial-specific fast transients keep the difference coordinate away from zero. If nonlinear dynamics rotate directions with state, no fixed V describes the entire trajectory. Near-one-dimensionality is a property of a particular data distribution and time window, not a claim that the network can access only one line forever.
keyPoints: Activity coordinates and mode coordinates are reversible representations of the same state.
After the fast mode decays, the slow mode dominates the trajectory and produces approximate low dimensionality.
The error from discarding a mode is quantified by the square of that mode's coordinate.
Persistent input, transients, or a nonlinear curved manifold can invalidate a fixed straight-line approximation.

derivation.title: Why the loss of a fast mode yields a nearly one-dimensional trajectory
derivation.setup: Assume the input is removed and both modes are stable, then compare their relative magnitudes over time.

steps.title: Write both exponential solutions
steps.explanation: Each decoupled mode decays according to its own time constant.

steps.title: Write the state reconstruction
steps.explanation: Multiply each scalar coordinate by its basis direction and add the two terms.

steps.title: Compare relative amplitudes
steps.explanation: If \(\tau -<\tau _{+}\), then \(|\alpha _{-}/\alpha +|\) contains the exponent \(-t(1/\tau _{-}-1/\tau _{+})\) and decreases with time.

steps.title: Obtain the one-dimensional approximation
steps.explanation: Once this ratio falls below a chosen tolerance, the relative error contributed by \(\alpha _{-}\) is small.

symbolNotes: The relative ratio is dimensionless and compares two coordinates in the same orthonormal basis.
If \(\alpha +(0)=0\), this ratio is undefined; use the residual-energy fraction directly.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\alpha \pm\) and h share the same units, while \(\xi \pm\) is dimensionless, so both terms in the reconstruction have compatible units.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\tau _{-}=\tau _{+}\), both modes decay at the same relative rate, so timescale separation does not automatically collapse the initial two-dimensional structure to one dimension.

workedExample.title: How quickly does the trajectory enter the low-dimensional manifold?
workedExample.problem: Let \(\alpha +(0)=4\), \(\alpha -(0)=2\), \(\tau _{+}=200 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(\tau _{-}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find both amplitudes and the difference-mode energy fraction after 100 ms.
workedExample.result: After 100 ms, well over 99.9% of the state energy lies on the common axis, so a one-dimensional approximation is safe.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Swapping 20 ms and 200 ms reverses the fast/slow conclusion; first check which denominator is closer to zero.

selfCheck.prompt: If a constant input \(\beta _{-}=1\) acts at every moment, must \(\alpha _{-}\) approach zero?
selfCheck.answer: No. A stable difference mode approaches the nonzero fixed point \(\alpha _{-}* = \beta _{-}/(1+w_{0})\), so the trajectory can remain away from the common axis. Low-dimensional conclusions depend on input structure.

pitfalls: Calling a coordinate transform itself dimensionality reduction; true reduction begins only when a coordinate is discarded.
Interpreting low dimensionality as activity in only a few neurons instead of coordinated variation of many neurons through a few population patterns.

modules.title: PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors
modules.guidingQuestion: Why must the direction of maximum variance be the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue of the centered covariance?
paragraphs: Now suppose W is unknown and we observe only T population vectors \(h_{t}\in \mathbb{R}^N\). First compute the \(\operatorname{mean} \bar{h}\) and define \(\delta h_{t}=h_{t}-\bar{h}\). The covariance \(C=(1/T)\sum _t \delta h_{t}\delta h_{t}^\mathrm{T}\) is an N×N symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix; \(C_{ij}\) describes centered cofluctuation between neurons i and j. For a chosen unit direction v, each sample has scalar projection \(p_{t}=v^\mathrm{T}\delta h_{t}\).

The projection variance is \((1/T)\sum  p_{t}^{2}=(1/T)\sum  v^\mathrm{T}\delta h_{t}\delta h_{t}^\mathrm{T}v=v^\mathrm{T}Cv\). Without a constraint on ||v||, scaling v arbitrarily would make the variance arbitrarily large, so require \(v^\mathrm{T}v=1\). Maximize \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv-\lambda (v^\mathrm{T}v-1)\) with a Lagrange multiplier. Differentiating with respect to every component of v gives \(2Cv-2\lambda v=0\), or \(Cv=\lambda v\). The candidate directions are therefore covariance eigenvectors.

Along eigenvector \(v_{k}\), projected variance equals \(\lambda _{k}\) because \(v_{k}^\mathrm{T}Cv_{k}=v_{k}^\mathrm{T}(\lambda _{k}v_{k})=\lambda _{k}\). Choosing \(v_{1}\) for the largest eigenvalue gives PC1. The derivation establishes only maximum data variance. A small but reliable task signal or a large measurement artifact can make PC1 poor for decoding, nor is it automatically a causal circuit direction.

Modes of W and PCs of C align only under additional conditions. For example, in a linear network driven by isotropic noise at stationarity, with W normal or symmetric, slow dynamical modes often accumulate more variance. Structured input, unequal noise, trial conditions, and nonlinear observations can all rotate the covariance. Similar axes motivate a hypothesis; statistical collinearity does not identify recurrent weights by itself.
keyPoints: PCA must be applied to centered activity: \(C=E[\delta h\delta h^\mathrm{T}]\).
Under a unit-norm constraint, projected variance is \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\).
A stationary point satisfies \(Cv=\lambda v\), and the eigenvector with the largest \(\lambda\) is PC1.
Maximum variance is not the same as maximum causal or behavioral relevance.

derivation.title: Rayleigh-quotient derivation of PC1
derivation.setup: Compute the variance of a one-dimensional projection of centered samples and maximize it subject to unit length.

steps.title: Expand the projection variance
steps.explanation: Because \(p=v^\mathrm{T}\delta h\) is scalar, \(p^{2}=v^\mathrm{T}\delta h\delta h^\mathrm{T}v\); averaging over samples gives \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\).

steps.title: Add the length constraint
steps.explanation: Construct \(L(v,\lambda )=v^\mathrm{T}Cv-\lambda (v^\mathrm{T}v-1)\) to prevent arbitrary rescaling.
steps.latex: \mathcal L=\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}C\mathbf v-\lambda(\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}\mathbf v-1)

steps.title: Differentiate with respect to v
steps.explanation: Because C is symmetric, the gradient is 2Cv; setting the gradient to zero yields the eigenproblem.

steps.title: Choose the largest candidate
steps.explanation: For a normalized eigenvector \(v_{k}\) the objective equals \(\lambda _{k}\), so choose the largest eigenvalue.

symbolNotes: \(\delta h\) and v are N×1; C is N×N; p and \(\lambda\) are scalars.
Using 1/(T-1) instead of 1/T for C leaves the eigenvectors unchanged and rescales every eigenvalue by the same constant.
derivation.unitsCheck: If h is a firing rate, C and \(\lambda\) have units of \(\mathrm{rate}^{2}\); v is dimensionless and projection p retains the rate unit.
derivation.limitCheck: If every sample is identical, centering gives \(C=0\). Variance is zero in every direction and the PC directions are not unique.

workedExample.title: Compute the PC of a two-dimensional covariance by hand
workedExample.problem: Given \(C=[[5,4],[4,5]]\), find both eigenvectors and eigenvalues, then interpret the long axis of the data cloud.
steps: For common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\), \(C(1,1)^\mathrm{T}=(9,9)^\mathrm{T}\), so the eigenvalue is 9.
For difference vector \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), \(C(1,-1)^\mathrm{T}=(1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), so the eigenvalue is 1.
After normalization, PC1=\((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\) and PC2=\((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\); the variance of PC1 is 9 times that of PC2.
workedExample.result: The data cloud is elongated along the common axis, where h1 and h2 vary together. Retaining PC1 explains \(9/(9+1)=90\)% of the variance.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The trace of C is 10, equal to the eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 9+1\), which checks the arithmetic.

selfCheck.prompt: What is chiefly mixed in if \(E[hh^\mathrm{T}]\) is computed without centering?
selfCheck.answer: The mean outer-product term \(\bar{h}\) \(\bar{h}^\mathrm{T}\) is included, so the leading direction may represent the mean firing pattern rather than trial or temporal fluctuations.

pitfalls: Calling covariance eigenvectors recurrent modes.
Forgetting to constrain \(||v||=1\), which leaves variance maximization unbounded.

modules.title: Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations
modules.guidingQuestion: When K PCs are retained, exactly what is preserved, and at what step is information lost?
paragraphs: Order the covariance eigenvalues \(\lambda _{1}\ge \lambda _{2}\ge \cdots \ge \lambda _{N}\) with orthonormal eigenvectors v1,...,vN. PC one uses v1. PC two must be orthogonal to v1 and maximize variance in the remaining subspace, so it uses v2. Continuing gives \(V_{K}=[v_{1},\cdots ,vK]\), an N×K matrix. For one centered sample, score vector \(p=V_{K}^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\) has K coordinates.

If all N components are retained, V is an orthogonal square matrix and \(h=\bar{h}+VV^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\); the transform is reversible and loses no information. With \(K<N\), reconstruction \(\hat{h}=\bar{h}+V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\) is the sample's orthogonal projection onto the top-K subspace. The discarded residual \(e=(I-V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T})(h-\bar{h})\) is orthogonal to the retained subspace.

Mean squared reconstruction error equals the sum of discarded eigenvalues \(\sum _{k>K}\lambda _{k}\). This is why PCA minimizes squared reconstruction error among all K-dimensional linear subspaces. Calling the reconstruction denoised requires an extra assumption: noise primarily occupies low-variance directions and signal occupies high-variance directions. A rare but important movement command on a low-variance axis would be treated as residual by PCA.

The practical algorithm has five steps: center across the neuron dimension; compute the N×N covariance or apply SVD to the data matrix; sort eigenpairs; project to obtain scores; and reconstruct or analyze for the task. Training and test data must use the training-set mean and PCs. Recomputing them separately and then comparing coordinates can turn a basis change into an apparent condition difference.
keyPoints: \(V_{K}\) is N×K, scores are K×1, and reconstruction returns to N×1 neuron space.
A complete orthogonal basis transform is lossless; dimensions are discarded only by projection with \(K<N\).
PCA residual error equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues.
'Denoising' assumes high-variance signal and low-variance noise; the name of the algorithm does not establish that assumption.

derivation.title: Top-K reconstruction and error
derivation.setup: Decompose a centered state in an orthonormal PC basis and separate retained from discarded terms.

steps.title: Compute scores
steps.explanation: Each score is the dot product of the sample with the corresponding unit PC.

steps.title: Retain the first K terms
steps.explanation: Multiply the first K scalar scores back into their basis vectors.

steps.title: Write the residual
steps.explanation: Expand the full state and subtract the retained terms, leaving only coordinates with \(k>K\).

steps.title: Average the residual energy
steps.explanation: Orthogonality removes cross terms, so \(E(p_{k}^{2})=\lambda _{k}\).

symbolNotes: The columns of \(V_{K}\) are N-dimensional unit vectors; p is a K-dimensional score vector.
\(\hat{h}\) and h have the same firing-rate units; \(\lambda _{k}\) and squared error both have units of \(\mathrm{rate}^{2}\).
derivation.unitsCheck: \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) has shape N×N and acts on N×1 centered activity. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I_{K}\), but \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is generally not \(I_{N}\).
derivation.limitCheck: At \(K=N\), residual and error are zero; at \(K=0\), reconstruction is only the mean and error equals total variance.

workedExample.title: Top-2 reconstruction of a three-dimensional state
workedExample.problem: Let \(\operatorname{mean}=0\), with PCs equal to coordinate axes \(v_{1}=(1,0,0)\), \(v_{2}=(0,1,0)\), \(v_{3}=(0,0,1)\), and sample \(h=(4,2,1)\). Retain \(K=2\).
steps: Keeping the first two terms gives \(\hat{h}=4v_{1}+2v_{2}=(4,2,0)\).
The residual is \(h-\hat{h}=(0,0,1)\), with squared error 1.
workedExample.result: Top-2 reconstruction keeps the first two coordinates and discards the third component. Whether this is denoising depends on whether the third axis is predominantly noise.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The original squared norm is 21, the reconstruction has 20, and the residual has 1, satisfying the orthogonal Pythagorean relation \(21=20+1\).

selfCheck.prompt: Why does \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I\) not imply \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}=I\)?
selfCheck.answer: When \(K<N\), \(V_{K}\) is not square. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}\) is the identity in K-space, while \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is the N-space projector onto a K-dimensional subspace.

pitfalls: Fitting PCA separately in each condition and comparing PC1 coordinates directly, despite possible rotation of the axes.
Assuming that a smoother reconstruction means the discarded activity was noise, without behavioral or held-out validation.

modules.title: Choosing dimensionality with the eigenvalue cliff and cumulative variance
modules.guidingQuestion: How should K be selected from the eigenvalue spectrum without treating a convenient cutoff as a natural constant?
paragraphs: A scree plot graphs sorted \(\lambda _{k}\) against component index k. If the first few eigenvalues are large and the curve then enters a flat tail, the transition is called an eigenvalue cliff or elbow. Directions before the cliff capture stronger coordinated variation; each direction after it contributes little additional variance. Real spectra often decline continuously, however, so different readers may place the elbow differently.

Cumulative variance explained \(F(K)=\sum _{k=1}^K\lambda _{k}/\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\) increases monotonically from \(F(0)=0\) to \(F(N)=1\). Its numerator must be \(\sum _{j=1}^K\lambda _{j}\) and its denominator the total variance \(\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\); writing only \(\lambda _{i}\) or omitting the denominator no longer represents cumulative explained variance. Thresholds of 80%, 90%, or 95% give reproducible rules but need not be optimal for a particular scientific question. Measurement noise can raise the tail, condition means can create large PCs, and trial averaging can change the spectrum. Report preprocessing and the selection criterion together with K.

A stronger dimensionality choice uses held-out data. Fit PCs on training trials and compare reconstruction error on test trials, or evaluate behavioral decoding, likelihood, or downstream model performance as K changes. A low-variance component may still deserve retention if it materially improves held-out behavior prediction. PCA dimensionality depends on both the data and the purpose of the analysis.

Finally separate three meanings of dimension. The number of slow dynamical modes of W follows from model stability; PCA dimension follows from the observed covariance spectrum; task dimension follows from behaviorally relevant variables. Carefully designed experiments can relate them, but no general identity equates them.
keyPoints: A scree-plot elbow is a heuristic and usually has no unique location.
Cumulative variance \(F(K)\) is the partial sum of sorted eigenvalues divided by their total sum.
A dimensionality choice should report preprocessing, threshold, and held-out criterion.
PCA dimension, dynamical dimension, and task dimension should not be used interchangeably.

derivation.title: Complementarity of cumulative variance and residual error
derivation.setup: Use the eigenvalue sum to express retained variance and discarded reconstruction error together.

steps.title: Define total variance
steps.explanation: The trace of the covariance equals the sum of all eigenvalues.

steps.title: Compute the retained fraction
steps.explanation: The mean squared amplitude carried by the top-K coordinates is the sum of the first K eigenvalues.

steps.title: Compute the discarded fraction
steps.explanation: Because the full fraction is 1, the unretained fraction is \(1-F(K)\).

steps.title: Connect to reconstruction error
steps.explanation: The normalized mean squared PCA residual equals the discarded variance fraction exactly.

symbolNotes: Every \(\lambda _{k}\ge 0\) because a covariance matrix is positive semidefinite.
\(F(K)\) is dimensionless and lies between 0 and 1; multiply by 100% to express it as a percentage.
derivation.unitsCheck: Numerator and denominator both have units of \(\mathrm{rate}^{2}\), so the ratio is unitless. K is an integer index, not a continuous parameter.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\lambda _{1}=\cdots =\lambda _{N}\), the spectrum has no cliff and \(F(K)=K/N\). Any low-dimensional cutoff then reflects an external tolerance rather than a natural turning point in the data.

workedExample.title: Different cutoffs produce different values of K
workedExample.problem: The eigenvalues are \([9,3,1,1]\). Find the smallest K under cumulative-variance thresholds of 80% and 95%.
steps: Total variance is 14; \(F(1)=9/14\approx 64.3\)%.
\(F(2)=12/14\approx 85.7\)%, so an 80% threshold selects \(K=2\).
\(F(3)=13/14\approx 92.9\)% and \(F(4)=100\)%, so a 95% threshold selects \(K=4\).
workedExample.result: The same data give \(K=2\) or \(K=4\) solely because the threshold changes. The cutoff is an analysis decision and must be reported explicitly.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Cumulative variance should never decrease and must equal 1 at \(K=N\). Violating either condition usually signals an error in sorting or the denominator.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does '95% variance explained' not guarantee retention of 95% of behavioral information?
selfCheck.answer: Variance measures activity amplitude, whereas behavioral information depends on condition distributions and the decoder. A low-variance direction may reliably distinguish choices, so the two percentages are not generally equivalent.

pitfalls: Treating a hand-drawn elbow as the one true neural dimensionality.
Reporting only a cumulative-variance threshold while omitting centering, trial averaging, noise treatment, and held-out validation.

objectives: Use synaptic-block logic to distinguish a cell-intrinsic pacemaker, a follower, and a network-generated half-center rhythm, while stating the limits of this experimental diagnosis.
Solve for the complex eigenvalues of a two-neuron rotation matrix, using the real and imaginary parts to assess envelope stability and oscillation frequency, respectively.
Explain every term in the Morris–Lecar voltage and recovery equations, then reconstruct the relaxation cycle from nullclines, fixed points, and fast–slow separation.
Distinguish intrinsic release from intrinsic escape in a reciprocally inhibitory half-center, identifying whose intrinsic transition triggers each phase switch.
Transfer the phase-plane geometry of a conductance model to a firing-rate model with adaptation while respecting the difference in model level.
prerequisiteBridge: Oscillation requires two separate questions: does the state move back and forth, and does its amplitude persist? A complex number \(z=a+ib\) can be viewed as horizontal and vertical coordinates in a plane. Euler's relation \(e^{ibt}=\cos(bt)+i \sin(bt)\) expresses rotation with sines and cosines. If a solution contains \(e^{(a+ib)t}\), a controls growth or decay of the envelope, whereas |b| controls angular frequency. Observing \(b\ne 0\) establishes a rotational component, not a sustained rhythm.

A two-dimensional phase plane represents each state as a point (V,N). The V-nullcline is the set where \(dV/dt=0\), and the N-nullcline is the set where \(dN/dt=0\); only their intersection is a fixed point. Away from the nullclines, the signs of \(dV/dt\) and \(dN/dt\) set the arrow direction. A nullcline is not a trajectory, and an intersection is not automatically stable: inspect whether nearby arrows approach or recede from it.

A fast–slow system contains one fast variable and one slow variable. In Morris–Lecar, membrane voltage V changes rapidly through current balance, whereas K activation or recovery N changes more slowly. A trajectory often drifts along a stable branch of the V-nullcline, then V jumps rapidly to the other branch at a fold. Once this slow-drift–fast-jump structure is understood, pacemaker relaxation oscillations, reciprocally inhibitory half-centers, and rate–adaptation oscillators can be compared in a common geometric language.

diagnostic.prompt: A neuron's linear mode has eigenvalue -2+6i s^-1. Does its amplitude grow or decay over time?
diagnostic.answer: The amplitude decays as \(e^{-2t}\); 6 rad/s specifies only the angular frequency of rotation.
diagnostic.explanation: Read the real part first to determine the envelope and the imaginary part second to determine oscillation. If you equated a complex eigenvalue with a sustained rhythm, review linear complex modes.

diagnostic.prompt: What does an intersection of the V-nullcline and N-nullcline represent?
diagnostic.answer: It simultaneously satisfies \(dV/dt=0\) and \(dN/dt=0\), so it is a fixed point of the two-dimensional system.
diagnostic.explanation: Stability still depends on the nearby vector field; an intersection alone does not tell you whether the point is stable, a saddle, or unstable.

diagnostic.prompt: After synapses are blocked, one cell continues at approximately its original rhythm. Which candidate mechanism does this most directly support?
diagnostic.answer: It supports a cell-intrinsic pacemaker mechanism in that cell, although drug side effects and residual coupling must still be controlled.
diagnostic.explanation: This is supporting evidence, not a logical proof; the diagnosis assumes a complete block that does not alter intrinsic currents.

diagnostic.prompt: What is the central criterion for distinguishing release from escape?
diagnostic.answer: Ask whether the active cell stops and lifts inhibition, or the inhibited cell recovers intrinsically, crosses a threshold, and escapes inhibition.
diagnostic.explanation: Do not look only at which cell spikes first. Track the intrinsic variable and nullcline crossing that trigger the transition.

modules.title: Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center
modules.guidingQuestion: How does persistence or loss of rhythm after synaptic block narrow the mechanisms, and why is it not sufficient proof by itself?
paragraphs: The source pages first distinguish two origins. A cell-intrinsic pacemaker continues to generate a rhythm from its own voltage-gated currents even without periodic synaptic input; a follower does not oscillate on its own and simply tracks synaptic drive from a pacemaker. The second origin is a network-generated rhythm: individual cells may remain tonic or silent in isolation, but reciprocal inhibition makes the pair alternate activity as a half-center oscillator. Respiration and alternating muscles during walking are the functional examples used in the course.

Synaptic block is an intervention, not a labeling exercise. If neuron 1 retains its rhythm after the block while neuron 2 becomes tonic or silent, the result is consistent with 1 as pacemaker and 2 as follower. If the pair alternates naturally but both lose rhythmicity under the block, the result supports a network-generated candidate. The key observation is each cell's time series in intact and blocked conditions, not a comparison of average frequency across different animals.

The experiment cannot eliminate every alternative explanation. A blocker may alter intrinsic conductances, the block may be incomplete, electrical coupling may remain, and sensory feedback may contribute in an intact preparation. A stronger design records membrane potential, verifies that synaptic current disappears, uses washout or a second blocking method, and tests whether current injection into an isolated cell can re-evoke the rhythm. State that the result supports a candidate mechanism, not that it proves a unique one.

A CPG is a central neural circuit capable of organizing patterned motor output without an external command at the same periodicity. The definition does not require real behavior to be independent of sensory feedback: sensory input can reset phase, adjust speed, or stabilize gait. Calling all rhythmic neural activity a CPG confuses an oscillator with sensory entrainment and downstream follower responses.
keyPoints: Persistence of intrinsic rhythm after a block supports a pacemaker; loss of alternation supports network dependence.
A synaptic-block result requires checks for block completeness and side effects on intrinsic currents.
The basic half-center motif is reciprocal inhibition with alternating phases.
A CPG can be modulated by sensory feedback; it does not imply open-loop behavior.

derivation.title: Compare mechanistic hypotheses with intervention outcomes
derivation.setup: List the predictions of all three candidate mechanisms under intact and synaptic-block conditions, then use the observations to rule out incompatible candidates.

steps.title: State the pacemaker prediction
steps.explanation: A pacemaker's intrinsic state variables generate its rhythm, so the cell should continue to oscillate after a complete block, although loss of tonic input may change its frequency.

steps.title: State the follower prediction
steps.explanation: Once its periodic drive is removed, a follower should not retain the original rhythm; it commonly becomes tonic, silent, or responsive only to injected pulses.

steps.title: State the half-center prediction
steps.explanation: Breaking mutual inhibition abolishes coordinated alternation. Whether either single cell still oscillates depends on whether it also has pacemaker currents.

steps.title: Add control conditions
steps.explanation: The observed contrast can identify the source of rhythm only after confirming loss of synaptic transmission and preservation of membrane health.

symbolNotes: Define 'persistence' with measurable quantities such as frequency, phase regularity, and waveform.
The mechanistic predictions concern counterfactual conditions in the same preparation.
derivation.unitsCheck: Measure frequency in Hz and period in s, with \(f=1/T\); when comparing after a block, use a sufficiently long recording window.
derivation.limitCheck: If both cells combine intrinsic oscillation with reciprocal inhibition, the block reveals a mixed mechanism rather than forcing the system into one category.

workedExample.title: Diagnose a candidate network from block results
workedExample.problem: In the intact preparation, cells A/B alternate at 2 Hz. After the block, A still oscillates at 1.8 Hz and B fires constantly. Give the minimal mechanism and the next control.
steps: Because A's rhythm is approximately preserved, first classify A as an intrinsic-pacemaker candidate.
B loses its modulation, consistent with a follower candidate. The intact alternation could arise from periodic drive from A to B or from more complex inhibition.
Next inject periodic current into B to verify that it can follow, measure synaptic current to confirm a complete block, and check whether the drug altered A's waveform.
workedExample.result: The minimal account is that A supplies intrinsic rhythmic drive and B follows it; this does not yet exclude feedback contributions from both A/B.
workedExample.sanityCheck: 1.8 Hz is close to but not identical to 2 Hz, reasonably suggesting that removing coupling changed the pacemaker frequency slightly rather than requiring exact equality.

selfCheck.prompt: If both cells stop alternating after the block but continue to oscillate at different frequencies, is this a purely network-generated rhythm?
selfCheck.answer: No. Coordinated alternation depends on network coupling, but each cell retains intrinsic oscillatory capacity; the full mechanism is coupled intrinsic oscillators.

pitfalls: Interpreting disappearance of the rhythm after a block as cell death without testing excitability.
Describing a CPG as a fully autonomous system unaffected by sensory feedback.

modules.title: Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does an imaginary eigenvalue component create back-and-forth variation, while intrinsic leak makes that variation decay?
paragraphs: The source page uses \(W=[[0,-w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\), with excitation in one coupling direction and inhibition in the other, so W formally resembles a two-dimensional rotation generator. The full rate equation remains \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), so continuous-time stability is set not by the ±iw0 eigenvalues of W alone, but by the eigenvalues \((-1\pm iw0)/\tau\) of \(A=(-I+W)/\tau\). Their real part is fixed at \(-1/\tau\), so the unforced envelope must decay.

The characteristic polynomial \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}+w_{0}^{2}=0\) gives λ_W=±i|w0|. A complex-mode solution contains \(e^{(-1\pm iw0)t/\tau }=e^{-t/\tau }[\cos(|w_{0}|t/\tau )\pm i \sin(|w_{0}|t/\tau )]\). Combining the conjugate pair yields real sine–cosine trajectories for h1 and h2. The angular frequency is \(\omega =|w_{0}|/\tau  \mathrm{rad}/s\), and the ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega /(2\pi )\).

In the phase plane, the trajectory rotates about the fixed point while its radius contracts as \(e^{-t/\tau }\), producing an inward spiral. A positive full real part instead produces an expanding outward spiral. With a real part exactly equal to zero, a linear system has neutrally stable closed orbits but no amplitude selection, so noise makes the radius drift. A stable autonomous limit cycle generally requires a nonlinearity that expands small amplitudes and contracts large ones.

Thus, having complex eigenvalues is not equivalent to having a sustained CPG rhythm. A complex pair means that the transient response to a perturbation may oscillate. Long-term rhythm additionally depends on the real part, nonlinear saturation, external drive, and noise. The notes turn next to Morris–Lecar precisely to introduce fast–slow geometry capable of producing a stable nonlinear cycle.
keyPoints: The full-system eigenvalues are \((-1\pm iw0)/\tau\); the ±iw0 eigenvalues of W alone are insufficient.
The real part determines the envelope, and the imaginary part determines angular frequency.
A negative real part produces an inward spiral and damped oscillation.
A stable limit cycle requires amplitude regulation; complex eigenvalues alone are not enough.

derivation.title: Solve the complex modes and recover a real oscillation
derivation.setup: First find the eigenvalues of W, then restore intrinsic leak and \(\tau\) in the continuous-time generator.

steps.title: Find the characteristic roots of W
Obtain the roots of the full generator
steps.explanation: For \(A=(-I+W)/\tau\), subtract 1 from each eigenvalue of W and then divide by \(\tau\).

steps.title: Apply Euler's relation
steps.explanation: Separate the complex exponential into a decaying envelope and sine/cosine rotation.

steps.title: Convert the frequency
steps.explanation: The imaginary part is in rad/s; divide by \(2\pi\) to obtain cycles/s.

symbolNotes: w0 is dimensionless; if \(\tau\) is in s, \(\lambda _{A}\) has units s^-1.
Complex eigenvectors are computational devices; a real firing-rate trajectory is formed by combining conjugate modes.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\omega\) has units rad/s and f has units Hz; the exponent in \(e^{-t/\tau }\) must be dimensionless.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(w_{0}=0\), \(\omega =0\) and the system only decays exponentially without oscillating; as \(\tau \to \infty\), both decay and rotation slow in this model.

workedExample.title: Read the waveform from the full eigenvalue
workedExample.problem: Given \(\tau =0.2 \mathrm{s}\) and \(w_{0}=4\), find the envelope time constant, angular frequency, frequency in Hz, and amplitude fraction after one period.
steps: The full eigenvalues are \((-1\pm 4i)/0.2=-5\pm 20i s^{-1}\).
The envelope time constant is \(1/5=0.2 \mathrm{s}\); \(f=20/(2\pi )\approx 3.18 \mathrm{Hz}\) and the period is ≈0.314 s.
After one period, the amplitude fraction is \(e^{-0.314/0.2}=e^{-1.57}\approx 0.208\).
workedExample.result: After one revolution the trajectory retains only about 20.8% of its initial amplitude, so this is a strongly damped transient, not a sustained oscillator.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The period comes from the imaginary part and the envelope from the real part; using \(|\lambda |\) for both gives inconsistent results.

selfCheck.prompt: What happens if the full eigenvalues are \(0.2\pm 5i s^{-1}\)?
selfCheck.answer: The trajectory rotates while its envelope grows as \(e^{0.2t}\), producing an outward spiral. The linear model is unstable; whether a limit cycle subsequently forms depends on nonlinear saturation.

pitfalls: Writing rad/s directly as Hz and forgetting to divide by \(2\pi\).
Reporting only the imaginary part while ignoring the -h leak in the full equation.

modules.title: Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points
modules.guidingQuestion: How do ionic-current equations generate a two-dimensional phase plane, and how can that plane identify resting and oscillatory candidates?
paragraphs: Morris–Lecar compresses conductance dynamics into two state variables, V and N. Its voltage equation is C dV/dt=-gL(V-EL)-gCa M∞(V)(V-ECa)-gK \(N(V-E_{K})+I_{e}\). Each \(g(V-E)\) is conductance times driving force; the preceding minus signs follow the outward-current convention. \(M_{\infty }(V)\) assumes fast Ca activation and therefore takes its voltage-dependent steady-state value immediately, whereas N follows \(N_{\infty }(V)\) on a slower time scale.

The recovery equation can be written \(\tau N dN/dt=N_{\infty }(V)-N\). When \(N<N_{\infty }\), \(dN/dt>0\) and K activation increases; when \(N>N_{\infty }\), it decreases. The N-nullcline is therefore the \(\operatorname{sigmoid} N=N_{\infty }(V)\). The V-nullcline is obtained by setting net membrane current to zero and is often cubic-like or N-shaped. Their intersection makes both derivatives zero and is a candidate equilibrium.

Read a phase plane by determining signs in each region. Whether \(dV/dt\) is positive on a given side of the V-nullcline must be checked with a test point, not guessed from the curve's appearance. Below the N-nullcline, usually \(N<N_{\infty }\) and arrows point upward; above it, arrows point downward. A fixed point is stable if nearby arrows converge, a saddle if one direction converges and another diverges, and unstable if the flow departs overall.

Fast–slow separation comes from the difference between the voltage time scale C/g and \(\tau N\). When V is fast, a trajectory quickly approaches an attracting branch of the V-nullcline, then N slowly carries it along that branch. If the fixed point lies in an unstable middle region, the state may not settle and instead jump between the two stable branches, forming a relaxation oscillation. The particular bifurcation depends on parameters; a hand-drawn nullcline diagram conveys mechanism, not universal numerical values.
keyPoints: The V equation balances leak, Ca, K, and external currents.
The V-nullcline satisfies \(dV/dt=0\); the N-nullcline satisfies \(N=N_{\infty }(V)\).
Nullcline intersections are fixed points; their stability still requires the vector field.
Fast voltage and slow recovery permit slow motion along a branch and a fast jump at a fold.

derivation.title: Derive both nullclines from current balance
derivation.setup: Set each derivative to zero while retaining the role of every conductance and reversal potential.

steps.title: Write the voltage balance
steps.explanation: Capacitive current equals applied current minus the leak, Ca, and K ionic currents.

steps.title: Find the V-nullcline
steps.explanation: Set \(dV/dt=0\) and isolate N. The resulting function of V is shaped by activation curves and driving forces.

steps.title: Find the N-nullcline
steps.explanation: Set \(\tau N dN/dt=N_{\infty }(V)-N=0\).

steps.title: Determine the arrows
steps.explanation: Choose a test point on either side of each nullcline, substitute it into \(F(V,N)\) and \(G(V,N)\), and record separately whether V and N increase or decrease.

symbolNotes: Measure V and E in mV and conductance in nS or \(\mathrm{mS}/\mathrm{cm}^{2}\); the convention for C and membrane area must be consistent.
N, \(M_{\infty }\), and \(N_{\infty }\) are dimensionless gating quantities between 0 and 1.
derivation.unitsCheck: Conductance×voltage has units of current, as does C dV/dt. Both sides of the recovery equation describe dimensionless change per unit time.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(g_{K}=0\), the formula that isolates N on the V-nullcline is invalid, and N no longer feeds back onto voltage; the two-dimensional oscillator mechanism changes accordingly.

workedExample.title: Use signs to determine motion at a phase-plane point
workedExample.problem: At a point above the V-nullcline, substitution gives \(dV/dt<0\); the same point lies below the N-nullcline. Determine its initial direction of motion.
steps: \(dV/dt<0\) means that V moves leftward.
Below the N-nullcline, \(N<N_{\infty }(V)\), so \(dN/dt>0\) and N moves upward.
The combined vector points up and left. If the trajectory crosses a nullcline at the next moment, reassess the signs.
workedExample.result: The instantaneous trajectory points up and left; it does not run along either nullcline.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Only the corresponding derivative is zero on a nullcline. Merely being 'above the V-nullcline' does not establish the sign of dV; the problem supplies the test-point sign.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is a nullcline not the neuron's actual trajectory?
selfCheck.answer: A nullcline is only the set of points where one derivative is instantaneously zero. The other variable usually continues to change, so the state crosses or moves nearby; only an intersection of both nullclines can remain stationary.

pitfalls: Treating a reversal potential as a fixed current and ignoring the driving force V-E.
Assigning arrows from the cubic curve's shape alone instead of checking regional signs in the equations.

modules.title: Relaxation cycles and phase geometry of a reciprocally inhibitory half-center
modules.guidingQuestion: How does slow recovery carry the state to a fold, and how does reciprocal inhibition organize this intrinsic geometry into alternating output?
paragraphs: When the fixed point is unstable and the V-nullcline has two attracting outer branches, a trajectory can cycle through four stages. On the low-V branch, V rapidly approaches the branch while N slowly decreases. At the lower fold, no nearby stable voltage solution remains, so V jumps rapidly to the high branch. Along the high branch, N slowly rises and strengthens hyperpolarizing K current. At the upper fold, V jumps rapidly back to the low branch. Repeating this sequence creates an autonomous relaxation oscillation.

Slow portions of the voltage trace correspond to motion along phase-plane branches; steep rises and falls correspond to fast jumps. The period is governed mainly by slow N evolution, whereas the duration of spike-like transitions is governed by fast V dynamics. Changing Ie or the conductances moves the nullclines and can place the fixed point on a stable branch, terminating the cycle. An oscillator is therefore a parameter-dependent attractor, not a single waveform.

A half-center couples two Morris–Lecar cells through mutual inhibition. For cell i, write the synaptic current as \(-gS_{\infty }(V_{j})(V_{i}-Es)\), with a relatively negative Es. When presynaptic cell j is in the high state, \(S_{\infty }\approx 1\) and pushes i's V-nullcline into its inhibited position. When j is low, \(S_{\infty }\approx 0\) and i regains its free nullcline. Alternation follows because each change in synaptic state rearranges the partner's geometry.

Even if the fixed point of each isolated cell is stable, mutual inhibition plus recovery can make the pair oscillate; conversely, not every mutually inhibitory pair oscillates. The system needs an intrinsic variable that evolves slowly in active and inhibited phases, a suitable synaptic threshold, and the right ordering of transitions. A sensory pulse can push one cell across a separatrix and reset phase without generating the rhythm itself.
keyPoints: A relaxation cycle has four stages: slow motion on the low branch, an upward jump, slow motion on the high branch, and a downward jump.
Slow recovery largely determines period; fast jumps determine the waveform edges.
An active presynaptic cell moves the partner's effective V-nullcline through inhibitory current.
A half-center rhythm requires cooperation between intrinsic recovery and synaptic switching.

derivation.title: The sign sequence around a four-stage trajectory
derivation.setup: Follow the cycle order labeled on the source page and use the signs of \(dV/dt\) and \(dN/dt\) to explain each segment.

steps.title: Slow motion on the lower branch
steps.explanation: V is already close to the attracting branch; slow positive or negative change in N carries the state toward the lower fold.

steps.title: Jump from lower to upper branch
steps.explanation: Past the fold there is no nearby attracting low-voltage solution, so fast \(dV/dt\) carries V to the high branch.

steps.title: Slow motion on the upper branch
steps.explanation: High V promotes N activation, strengthening K current and moving the state toward the upper fold.

steps.title: Jump from upper to lower branch
steps.explanation: At the upper fold the high-voltage solution disappears, so fast V returns to the low branch and the sequence restarts.

symbolNotes: 'Upper/lower branch' refers to V; whether N rises or falls must be checked from the actual arrow field.
Cycle orientation depends on coordinates and parameters; do not assume clockwise motion without the original equations.
derivation.unitsCheck: The phase-plane axes are mV and dimensionless N. Elapsed time cannot be inferred from geometric distance alone.
derivation.limitCheck: If fast–slow separation disappears, a cycle may remain, but the approximation of slow branch motion and fast fold jumps becomes less accurate.

workedExample.title: Predict the effect of increasing the recovery time constant
workedExample.problem: Keep the nullcline shapes fixed and increase \(\tau N\) from 100 ms to 300 ms. Predict the main changes in period and fast-jump duration.
steps: Slow motion along the branches becomes about three times slower because \(dN/dt\) is reduced.
Because the cycle spends most of its time on the slow branches, its period lengthens substantially, approximately in proportion to \(\tau N\).
Fast V jumps are governed mainly by C and the conductances, so their duration should not also increase threefold.
workedExample.result: Frequency should decrease and waveform plateaus should lengthen, with comparatively small changes in the edge of each fast jump.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If the parameter change alters fixed-point stability or branch range, the simple proportional prediction fails; the problem explicitly holds the shapes fixed.

selfCheck.prompt: Why can two mutually inhibitory cells generate a network rhythm even when neither oscillates in isolation?
selfCheck.answer: Inhibition switches each partner's effective nullcline between active and inactive conditions. Slow recovery makes the cells reach their transitions in turn, so coupling creates periodic state switching.

pitfalls: Treating the fast jump as motion along a nullcline; the state leaves the slow manifold during a jump.
Assuming mutual inhibition alone is sufficient without checking the recovery variable and threshold ordering.

modules.title: Intrinsic release and intrinsic escape: what triggers the phase switch?
modules.guidingQuestion: When two cells alternate firing, how can we tell whether the active cell lets go or the inhibited cell escapes?
paragraphs: The source page simplifies the synapse with a sharp threshold: \(S_{\infty }(V)=0\) when \(V<VT\) and 1 when \(V>VT\). While the active cell's V exceeds VT, it inhibits its partner; once V falls below VT, inhibition shuts off rapidly. A free neuron follows the \(F(V,N)=0\) nullcline, whereas an inhibited neuron follows a shifted nullcline that includes synaptic current. Switching between these two geometries makes the identity of the first threshold-crosser an observable mechanistic criterion.

In a release mechanism, N rises while the active cell occupies the upper branch until that cell can no longer sustain high V. It jumps first to the low branch and falls below VT, closing the synapse; only then is the partner released to jump into its own high state. The trigger is intrinsic adaptation in the active cell. Clamping its recovery variable should delay or prevent the phase switch.

In an escape mechanism, N in the inhibited cell gradually recovers during the low state. Eventually that cell crosses the fold or separatrix of the inhibited nullcline and jumps high even while inhibition remains on. Its rise then inhibits the formerly active cell. The trigger is intrinsic recovery in the inhibited cell, so changing that recovery speed should strongly alter phase duration.

Real circuits can occupy a mixed regime: the active cell may be nearing release while its partner is nearing escape, leaving noise or sensory input to decide which occurs first. Experimentally, track both cells' voltage and a proxy for recovery before the transition, and use brief pulses to push the active cell down or the inhibited cell up. An alternating spike raster alone does not reveal causal order.
keyPoints: A sharp \(S_{\infty }\) threshold approximates the synapse as an on/off switch.
Release is triggered by intrinsic termination of the active cell.
Escape is triggered when intrinsic recovery in the inhibited cell crosses a boundary.
In mixed regimes, noise can make both mechanisms contribute to phase timing.

derivation.title: Distinguish release from escape by threshold-crossing order
derivation.setup: Decompose the last portion before a phase switch into three events: presynaptic threshold crossing, the inhibited-cell fold crossing, and the change in synaptic state.

steps.title: Define synaptic state
steps.explanation: Inhibition is on when \(V_{\mathrm{pre}}>VT\) and off when \(V_{\mathrm{pre}}<VT\).

steps.title: Check release ordering
steps.explanation: If active-cell V first falls below VT, S changes from 1 to 0, and the partner then jumps upward, release dominates.

steps.title: Check escape ordering
steps.explanation: If the partner crosses its inhibited threshold and jumps while S is still 1, then inhibits the formerly active cell, escape dominates.

steps.title: Propose an intervention
steps.explanation: Selectively slowing adaptation in the active cell should lengthen a release cycle; slowing recovery in the inhibited cell should lengthen an escape cycle.

symbolNotes: VT is a voltage threshold, and \(S_{\infty }\) is dimensionless.
'First' must be defined relative to temporal resolution and synaptic delay.
derivation.unitsCheck: The synaptic term \(gS(V-Es)\) has units of current; Heaviside S merely selects whether the conductance is on.
derivation.limitCheck: If synaptic activation is graded rather than sharp, there is no unique on/off time. Compare the rise in conductance with the timing of intrinsic transitions.

workedExample.title: Infer the switch mechanism from event times
workedExample.problem: A is active. At \(t=500 \mathrm{ms}\), B suddenly depolarizes while inhibition remains strong; at \(t=507 \mathrm{ms}\), A is inhibited; at \(t=512 \mathrm{ms}\), A falls below VT. Which mechanism dominates?
steps: B depolarizes before A falls below VT, so B did not wait for inhibition to shut off before rising.
B then inhibits A, consistent with the inhibited cell actively escaping its low state.
Classify the event as escape-dominant and test whether manipulating B's recovery variable changes the 500 ms latency.
workedExample.result: The event order supports intrinsic escape rather than release by the active cell.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Confirm that synaptic conductance was still high when B depolarized; A's spikes alone may underestimate the actual conductance offset.

selfCheck.prompt: If the active cell falls below VT and its partner jumps 20 ms later, does that delay refute release?
selfCheck.answer: No. Release requires only that removal of inhibition be the upstream trigger. The partner still takes finite time to leave its low state according to its own membrane and recovery dynamics.

pitfalls: Naming the mechanism solely from which cell spikes first, without measuring synaptic state.
Treating release and escape as mutually exclusive and ignoring mixed regimes and stochastic switching.

modules.title: From a conductance oscillator to a rate–adaptation half-center
modules.guidingQuestion: After removing ion-channel detail, what is the smallest set of rate-level variables that preserves half-center geometry?
paragraphs: Page 6 gives only the direction of the extension: replace V with firing rate h and N with an adaptation or recovery variable a while retaining similar nullcline geometry. A minimal pair can be written \(\tau _{h} dh_{i}/dt=-h_{i}+F(I_{i}-w h_{j}-a_{i})\), \(\tau a da_{i}/dt=-a_{i}+b h_{i}\). F is a thresholding, saturating nonlinearity; \(w>0\) denotes reciprocal inhibition; and b controls how activity accumulates adaptation.

While cell i is active, high \(h_{i}\) slowly raises \(a_{i}\). Increasing adaptation lowers effective drive until the active rate falls. Inhibition of the partner then weakens, allowing it to rise and subsequently inhibit the original cell. This is release-like switching. If \(a_{j}\) falls during the inhibited cell's low-activity phase, restoring its effective excitability until it crosses threshold first, switching is escape-like.

The rate model preserves state-dependent feedback, slow recovery, and threshold geometry; it does not preserve particular Ca/K currents, spike waveforms, or reversal potentials. It is suited to population rhythm, phase relations, and parameter effects, but one rate variable cannot establish a particular ionic mechanism. Parameters also change meaning across levels: \(\tau _{h}\) is a rate-response time, not a time constant obtained directly from membrane capacitance.

Validate the model by plotting \(h_{i}-a_{i}\) nullclines, simulating both rates, varying w, b, and \(\tau a\), and testing phase resetting. If F is fully linear and lacks saturation, strong feedback may produce only decay or divergence. Nonlinearity limits amplitude and permits a stable cycle. A rate-level fit can show compatibility with a computational mechanism but cannot uniquely identify cellular conductances.
keyPoints: A rate–adaptation model needs at least fast activity, slow recovery, reciprocal inhibition, and a nonlinearity.
Accumulating adaptation can trigger release; recovery during low activity can support escape.
A rate variable and a voltage or gating variable are not the same biological quantity.
Test the model through predictions of phase, frequency, resetting, and perturbations.

derivation.title: Feedback chain of a minimal rate half-center
derivation.setup: Starting from a pair of fast rate equations and slow adaptation equations, follow one phase switch step by step.

steps.title: Write the fast rate equations
steps.explanation: Each rate receives tonic input, inhibition from its partner, and its own adaptation.

steps.title: Write slow adaptation
steps.explanation: Activity drives \(a_{i}\) upward; without activity, \(a_{i}\) decays.

steps.title: Follow the active phase
steps.explanation: High h1 slowly raises a1; h2 is suppressed by w h1 while a2 gradually falls.

steps.title: Reach the switch
steps.explanation: The rates rapidly exchange high and low states when cell1's effective drive falls below the threshold of F or cell2 recovers to threshold.

symbolNotes: Depending on F, h may be a normalized rate or have units of Hz; a and I must share the same effective-input units.
For clear fast–slow alternation, \(\tau a\) should be substantially larger than \(\tau _{h}\).
derivation.unitsCheck: If h and the output of F are in Hz, every term is in Hz and division by \(\tau\) gives Hz/s. The quantities a, I, and w h must be addable.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(b=0\), activity no longer builds adaptation. Pure reciprocal inhibition without another slow process usually loses stable alternation.

workedExample.title: Predict rhythm from a parameter change
workedExample.problem: The model initially has \(\tau _{h}=20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(\tau a=400 \mathrm{ms}\). Double only \(\tau a\) to 800 ms, keeping all else fixed and assuming the cycle persists. Predict frequency and phase relation.
steps: Both slow adaptation and recovery become slower, so the active phase generally lengthens.
Because the two cells remain structurally symmetric, they should stay approximately in antiphase rather than acquire a fixed phase bias.
The period is governed mainly by the slow process and should increase, so frequency decreases, though it need not be exactly halved.
workedExample.result: Alternation should persist with a longer period and lower frequency. The exact ratio requires numerical simulation because the switching threshold and nonlinear F also matter.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Because \(\tau _{h}\) is unchanged, the edge of each fast rate transition should not stretch by the same factor as the plateau.

selfCheck.prompt: Why are two linear rate variables h1 and h2 usually insufficient for a stable half-center limit cycle?
selfCheck.answer: A linear system can only decay, rotate neutrally, or grow; it lacks a slow state and amplitude regulation. Adaptation or recovery plus nonlinear F supplies phase switching and a bounded cycle.

pitfalls: Naming a in the rate model as a particular K channel without additional evidence.
Inferring a half-center from one rate trace without verifying antiphase activity and perturbation responses in the partner.

objectives: Explain why integrating an eye-velocity command requires a persistent neural state after a saccade, and connect bilateral excitation/inhibition to left–right position tuning.
Derive the characteristic equation, eigenvalue-one constraint, and compensating weight family for a general \(2\times 2\) recurrent matrix, while also checking transverse stability.
Use the inverse of a measured F–I curve and fixed synaptic nonlinearities to construct a design matrix, turning an apparently nonlinear circuit fit into row-wise least squares.
Use the eigendecomposition of a quadratic loss Hessian to explain stiff and sloppy directions, parameter compensation, and an ensemble of adequate models.
Distinguish low dimensionality in neural-state space, sloppiness in parameter space, measurement uncertainty, and genuine biological degeneracy.
prerequisiteBridge: Integration turns velocity into position. If velocity is approximately constant during each short interval \(\Delta t\), the position change is about \(v\Delta t\). Summing many small intervals and taking the continuous limit gives \(x(t)=x(0)+\int v(t')dt'\). After a saccade, the velocity command returns to zero but eye position must not, so a neural circuit has to retain the integrated result. When a linear recurrent mode approaches eigenvalue 1, positive feedback nearly cancels intrinsic leak and creates a long time scale.

A two-by-two matrix W has two eigenvalues. In the rate equation \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), a mode's effective leak is \(1-\lambda\). Perfect linear integration requires at least one task-relevant eigenvalue equal to 1. The other eigenvalue must also lie in the stable range; otherwise the network retains state along the memory direction but explodes in the transverse direction. One functional constraint generally does not determine every synaptic weight uniquely.

Least squares chooses parameters that minimize squared differences between predicted and observed targets. If predictions depend linearly on the weights, the loss surface is a quadratic bowl whose Hessian gives curvature along different parameter directions. Large curvature means a small displacement greatly increases loss and is called stiff; small curvature permits a large displacement with little loss and is called sloppy. These directions live in parameter space, not along neural activity trajectories.

diagnostic.prompt: A constant eye velocity of 20 deg/s lasts 0.1 s. What position change does an ideal integrator predict?
diagnostic.answer: The change is \(20\times 0.1=2 \mathrm{deg}\).
diagnostic.explanation: Velocity times time gives position. If deg/s and s do not cancel in your units, review the velocity-to-position module.

diagnostic.prompt: Why is it insufficient merely to confirm that W has eigenvalue 1?
diagnostic.answer: The other modes must be stable, the task input must project onto the integrating mode, the readout must access it, and the nonlinear operating range must be adequate.
diagnostic.explanation: Eigenvalue one is only a local linear memory condition; it says nothing by itself about transverse stability or biological feasibility.

diagnostic.answer: No, division by zero is invalid. The integrator condition becomes \((1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})=0\), so at least one of W11 and W22 must equal 1.
diagnostic.explanation: The family formula assumes \(W_{12}\ne 0\). Special structures must be analyzed directly with \(\det(I-W)=0\).

diagnostic.prompt: What does a large Hessian eigenvalue mean?
diagnostic.answer: Loss has high curvature along the corresponding parameter combination, so a small parameter change substantially worsens the fit; that direction is stiff.
diagnostic.explanation: It does not mean that one corresponding synapse is large, nor that the direction is a principal component of neural activity.

modules.title: Eye-velocity integration, persistent position, and the bilateral circuit
modules.guidingQuestion: How does a brief saccade command become an eye-position code that persists after the command disappears?
paragraphs: Moving the eye requires phasic motor drive to generate velocity and tonic drive to oppose orbital restoring forces and hold the new position. The course abstracts the distributed brainstem and cerebellar network as a neural integrator: its input is the eye-velocity command \(v(t)\), and its output state approximates \(x(t)=x(0)+\int v(t')dt'\). Ideally, x retains its latest value when v returns to zero; if the network leaks, position slowly drifts back toward center.

The source diagram contains excitatory populations EL and ER and inhibitory populations IL and IR in the left and right hemispheres. Their position-tuning curves have opposite directions: at rightward positions, firing rises in one population and falls in the other. Mutual excitation can prolong the memory mode, while crossed inhibition organizes the left–right push–pull pattern into a signed coordinate. This is a functional architecture; arrows alone do not reveal the strength of each real synapse.

Linear tuning lets a weighted difference of population rates encode eye position. If a right-preferring neuron has \(hR\approx b+kx\) and a left-preferring one \(hL\approx b-kx\), then \(hR-hL\approx 2kx\), while the common baseline \(hR+hL\approx 2b\). The integrator can store signed position in a difference-like mode while keeping the common mode stable. Real neurons have thresholds, saturation, and heterogeneity, so these linear relations hold only over an operating range.

Test the integrator by asking whether firing persists after a velocity pulse, whether the persistent level scales with the pulse integral, and how a network perturbation changes the drift time constant. Position-tuning correlations alone cannot separate sensory eye-position feedback from recurrent memory; comparisons in darkness, feedback perturbations, or circuit interventions are needed.
keyPoints: The time integral of velocity gives position change.
Recurrent positive feedback sustains a persistent state after the command ends.
Opponent tuning in left and right populations can encode signed eye position.
Position-tuning correlations alone do not prove recurrent integration.

derivation.title: From velocity samples to a continuous position integral
derivation.setup: First accumulate position changes in finite time steps, then introduce continuous notation and a leaky neural implementation.

steps.title: Discrete accumulation
steps.explanation: During interval n, position increases by \(v_{n}\Delta t\).

steps.title: Sum all intervals
steps.explanation: The total change from 0 to t is the sum of the increment in each interval.

steps.title: Take the continuous limit
steps.explanation: As \(\Delta t\) shrinks, the Riemann sum approaches an integral.

steps.title: Connect to a neural mode
steps.explanation: Implement leaky integration with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}} d\alpha /dt=-\alpha +k v\); when \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) is long, the state is approximately retained over a delay.

symbolNotes: Use deg/s for v and deg for x; k maps the units of the velocity command into a neural coordinate.
\(\alpha\) is a population-mode amplitude and need not equal mechanical position.
