derivation.unitsCheck: v×dt gives deg, so the integral has the same units as x. In a rate-coordinate neural equation, k must supply any missing units.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\to \infty\) with appropriately scaled input, the system approaches a perfect integrator; with finite \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\), \(\alpha\) drifts exponentially under zero input.

workedExample.title: Accumulate two saccade commands
workedExample.problem: Start at \(x=0 \mathrm{deg}\). Move right at 30 deg/s for 0.08 s, then left at -20 deg/s for 0.05 s. Ignoring leak, find the final position.
steps: The first change is \(30\times 0.08=+2.4 \mathrm{deg}\).
The second change is \(-20\times 0.05=-1.0 \mathrm{deg}\).
The final position is \(x=0+2.4-1.0=+1.4 \mathrm{deg}\), still rightward.
workedExample.result: After the second command ends, an ideal integrator should hold +1.4 deg rather than return to zero.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Signs of velocity must match left–right direction. The total command area \(2.4-1.0=1.4 \mathrm{deg}\) provides a direct check.

selfCheck.prompt: If position returns to center after the velocity command with a time constant of 5 s, is this still an integrator?
selfCheck.answer: It is a leaky rather than perfect integrator. Behavior may appear persistent for periods shorter than 5 s, but a long delay reveals measurable drift.

pitfalls: Conflating velocity tuning and position tuning as the same population signal.
Treating the bilateral arrows in the schematic as the one measured connectomic implementation.

modules.title: General \(2\times 2\) weights, eigenvalue one, and a compensating family
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does retaining one mode impose only one weight constraint, allowing many different circuits to implement the same integration?
paragraphs: Let \(W=[[W_{11},W_{12}],[W_{21},W_{22}]]\). Its characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda ^{2}-(W_{11}+W_{22})\lambda +(W_{11}W_{22}-W_{12}W_{21})=0\), and the quadratic formula gives both eigenvalues. For \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh\), perfect integration requires an eigenvalue of W equal to 1 because that mode's coefficient \(-(1-\lambda )\) is exactly zero. Substituting \(\lambda =1\) directly is more robust than manipulating the square root and gives \(\det(I-W)=0\).

Expanding gives \(\det(I-W)=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})-W_{12}W_{21}=0\). If \(W_{12}\ne 0\), solve \(W_{21}=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})/W_{12}\). Once three weights are chosen, the fourth compensates; increasing a self-weight can be offset by changing cross-coupling while preserving \(\lambda =1\). This is a many-to-one functional mapping: different parameter points share the same integrator eigenvalue.

Do not hide special cases with division. When \(W_{12}=0\), the formula is invalid and the condition becomes \((1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})=0\), so at least one self-weight equals 1. The other eigenvalue must also be checked. Since the sum of the eigenvalues is \(\operatorname{trace}(W)\), if \(\lambda _{1}=1\) then \(\lambda _{2}=W_{11}+W_{22}-1\). Transverse stability of the continuous rate equation requires \(\lambda _{2}<1\). If \(\lambda _{2}\) is also very close to 1, the network acquires another slow mode and may fail to encode position uniquely.

Algebraic satisfaction does not guarantee biological feasibility. Excitatory and inhibitory cell types constrain weight signs, conductance and firing ranges constrain magnitudes, noise makes exact \(\lambda =1\) difficult to maintain, and nonlinear saturation changes large-state dynamics. Study the region of parameter space that gives adequate integration and its robustness, rather than treating a one-parameter relation as a complete circuit solution.
keyPoints: A perfect linear integrator satisfies \(\det(I-W)=0\).
The other eigenvalue must be stable; \(\lambda _{2}=\operatorname{trace}(W)-1\).
Parameter compensation is not measurement noise and does not guarantee biophysical feasibility.

derivation.title: From the characteristic polynomial to an integrator family
derivation.setup: Keep the matrix general rather than assuming symmetry, and handle the boundary case for division separately.

steps.title: Write the characteristic polynomial
steps.explanation: The two-by-two determinant produces the trace–determinant form.

steps.title: Set the memory eigenvalue to 1
steps.explanation: Substitute \(\lambda =1\) and rearrange.

steps.title: Solve the compensating relation
steps.explanation: Isolate W21 only when W12 is nonzero.

steps.title: Check the transverse root
steps.explanation: Because the roots sum to the trace, the other root is the trace minus 1.

symbolNotes: Wij are dimensionless effective recurrent gains.
Eigenvalue 1 belongs to W; the corresponding root of the full generator is \((\lambda -1)/\tau\).
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\det(I-W)\) is dimensionless. \(\tau\) appears only when converting an eigenvalue gap into a time constant.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(W_{12}\to 0\), the family formula becomes numerically unbounded, signaling that one should return to the undivided constraint rather than infer an infinite synapse.

workedExample.title: Solve for the fourth weight and check stability
workedExample.problem: Let \(W_{11}=0.8\), \(W_{22}=0.7\), and \(W_{12}=0.2\). Find W21 so that one mode is a perfect integrator, then check the other mode.
steps: The other eigenvalue is \(0.8+0.7-1=0.5\).
Its full transverse coefficient is \(-(1-0.5)/\tau =-0.5/\tau\), so that mode decays stably.
workedExample.result: \(W=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]]\) has eigenvalues 1 and 0.5, giving one memory mode and one stable transverse mode.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The \(\operatorname{trace} 1.5\) equals 1+0.5, and the determinant 0.5 equals \(1\times 0.5\), providing two checks.

selfCheck.prompt: What happens if the same constraint gives \(\lambda _{2}=1.1\)?
selfCheck.answer: The memory mode still has \(\lambda =1\), but the transverse mode's full growth rate is \((1.1-1)/\tau >0\). Any small error grows, so the full network is not a stable, usable integrator.

pitfalls: Replacing the general matrix with the symmetric two-neuron special case and missing asymmetric compensation.
Checking \(\det(I-W)=0\) without checking \(\lambda _{2}\), input projection, and readout.

modules.title: Biological variability and reparameterizing a nonlinear circuit fit
modules.guidingQuestion: Once nonlinear F–I and synaptic transfer functions are fixed, how can a model containing them become linear in its fitted weights?
paragraphs: Following work by Goldman, Marder, and others, the source page emphasizes that different parameter settings can produce similar voltage or behavioral dynamics; variability across animals need not destroy function. Approximately linear position tuning in the oculomotor integrator lets researchers measure rates at several eye positions and ask which sets of synaptic weights reproduce those states. This variability concerns model or individual parameters, not recording noise.

For postsynaptic neuron i, measure the target rate \(h_{i}(p\mu )\) at position \(p\mu\) and use the measured inverse F–I curve to convert it into the required net current \(Y_{i}\mu =F_{i}^{-1}(h_{i}(p\mu ))\). For each presynaptic neuron j, pass its rate through a fixed synaptic nonlinearity \(S_{E}\) or \(S_{I}\) to obtain feature \(X_{j}\mu\). Add a row of constant 1 values for bias current. The complicated biophysics is thereby precomputed into Y and X.

With the nonlinear functions fixed, the prediction is \(\hat{Y}_{i\mu }=\sum _j W_{ij} X_{j}\mu\), linear in the unknown weights Wij and bias. Each output neuron i can fit one row of weights independently. If M sample positions are columns, X has shape D×M, Y is N×M, W is N×D, and \(\hat{Y}=WX\) is dimensionally consistent. State this orientation explicitly, because placing samples in rows yields a transposed formula.

The boundary of this reparameterization matters. If the inverse F–I estimate is wrong, the synaptic threshold is fitted jointly, features are highly correlated, or noise is heteroscedastic, simple OLS gives unreliable uncertainty. Different nonlinear assumptions can yield different weight ensembles that fit the rates equally well. 'Linearized fitting' is a conditional computational convenience, not a claim that the native circuit lacks nonlinearities.
keyPoints: First use \(F_{i}^{-1}\) to convert each target rate into required current.
Once synaptic nonlinearities are fixed, their outputs become design-matrix features.
With samples as columns, \(Y=N\times M\), \(X=D\times M\), and \(W=N\times D\).
Linear in the weights does not mean that the entire biological model is linear.

derivation.title: From a steady-state circuit equation to \(Y=WX\)
derivation.setup: At every measured position, evaluate the known nonlinear terms first and leave only the weights unknown.

steps.title: Construct target current
steps.explanation: For every output i and sample \(\mu\), evaluate the inverse F–I curve.

steps.title: Construct the features
steps.explanation: Pass every presynaptic rate through its E or I synaptic function, then append a constant bias feature.

steps.title: Write the linear prediction
steps.explanation: The weights appear only as coefficients of the features.

steps.title: Stack into matrices
steps.explanation: Arrange all outputs and positions simultaneously.

symbolNotes: M is the number of positions/samples, D is the number of features including bias, and N is the number of output neurons.
Signs for E and I can be placed in constraints on W or in feature definitions, but the convention must remain consistent.
derivation.unitsCheck: \((N\times D)(D\times M)=N\times M\), matching Y; every column corresponds to the same eye position.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(F_{i}\) is not invertible or the rate lies on a saturation plateau, \(F_{i}^{-1}\) is not unique and target-current construction fails.

workedExample.title: Build one design row and predict current
workedExample.problem: At two positions, an output has features \(x_{1}=[1,2]\) and \(x_{2}=[3,1]\), with an additional bias 1 at both. The weights are \([w_{1},w_{2},b]=[0.5,-1,2]\). Find both predictions.
steps: At position 1, the feature vector is (1,2,1) and the prediction is \(0.5\times 1-1\times 2+2=0.5\).
At position 2, the feature vector is (3,1,1) and the prediction is \(0.5\times 3-1\times 1+2=2.5\).
workedExample.result: The target-current predictions at the two positions are 0.5 and 2.5; matrix and term-by-term calculations agree.
workedExample.sanityCheck: W has shape \(1\times 3\) and X has shape \(3\times 2\), so the output must be \(1\times 2\). An answer of \(2\times 1\) indicates that sample orientation was reversed.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does fitting become linear after fixing the nonlinearities even though the neuron response itself remains nonlinear?
selfCheck.answer: \(S_{j}\) and \(F_{i}^{-1}\) already apply nonlinear transformations to the data. Only the unknown weights linearly combine those transformed features; the full input–output mapping remains nonlinear.

pitfalls: Treating parameter variability and observation noise as the same source.
Applying \(YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\) without stating sample orientation and obtaining incompatible shapes.

modules.title: Least squares, the closed-form solution, and the Hessian
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does a squared-error fit form a quadratic surface, and how does the Hessian arise from the data design?
paragraphs: With samples as columns, write the loss \(L(W)=1/2||Y-WX||_F^{2}\). The Frobenius norm sums squared residuals across all outputs and samples. Output rows are independent, so begin with one weight row w and target row y: \(L(w)=1/2(y-wX)(y-wX)^\mathrm{T}\). Expanding gives the constant \(yy^\mathrm{T}\), the linear term \(-yX^\mathrm{T}w^\mathrm{T}\), and the quadratic term wXX^\(Tw^\mathrm{T}\).

Differentiating with respect to w gives gradient \((wX-y)X^\mathrm{T}\). Setting it to zero gives the normal equation wXX^\(T=yX^\mathrm{T}\). If \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is invertible, \(\hat{w}=yX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\); stacking all rows gives \(\hat{W}=YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\). If features are collinear, \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is singular and requires a pseudoinverse, regularization, or redesigned samples.

Near the optimum, let \(\Delta w=w-\hat{w}\). The normal equation eliminates the cross term, leaving \(L=L\min+1/2 \Delta w H \Delta w^\mathrm{T}\) with \(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\). The same feature Hessian applies row by row to the full W, or appears in blocks after vectorizing the parameters. H depends only on design features for this local curvature; changing the noise model or constraints changes the effective Hessian.

This connects fitting with experimental design. If one feature combination barely changes across positions, X contains little information along that direction and H has a small eigenvalue. Conditions that selectively activate that combination can increase curvature and tighten parameter uncertainty. Sloppiness need not be accepted passively; perturbations and improved sampling can reduce it.
keyPoints: The OLS loss is \(1/2||Y-WX||^{2}\).
When the inverse exists, \(\hat{W}=YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\).
\(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\) describes parameter curvature supported by the features.
Collinear features make H singular or nearly singular, requiring regularization or new experiments.

derivation.title: From quadratic loss to the OLS closed form
derivation.setup: Derive one output row first; multiple outputs simply repeat the calculation side by side.

steps.title: Write the loss
steps.explanation: The residual row is y-wX.

steps.title: Compute the gradient
steps.explanation: Differentiate with respect to each weight and collect the results as a row vector.

steps.title: Solve the normal equation
steps.explanation: Set the gradient to zero, then right-multiply by the inverse.

steps.title: Identify the Hessian
steps.explanation: Differentiate the gradient once more with respect to w.

symbolNotes: w is 1×D, X is D×M, y is 1×M, and H is D×D.
For multiple outputs, W is N×D and the formula applies to every row simultaneously.
derivation.unitsCheck: \((1\times D)(D\times M)=1\times M\), and \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is D×D. Every term in the loss has squared target-current units.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(M<D\) or the features are linearly dependent, \(\operatorname{rank}(XX^\mathrm{T})<D\) and the ordinary inverse does not exist. A pseudoinverse selects a minimum-norm solution but does not remove the identifiability problem.

workedExample.title: Identifiability from a two-feature Hessian
workedExample.problem: Let \(X=[[1,0,1],[0,1,1]]\). Compute \(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\) and determine whether it is invertible.
steps: \(\det(H)=4-1=3>0\), so H is invertible; its eigenvalues are 3 and 1.
workedExample.result: Both parameter combinations are identifiable, but curvature along the common-feature direction is 3 and exceeds the difference-direction curvature of 1.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The \(\operatorname{trace} 4\) must equal the eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 3+1\), and the determinant 3 must equal the product \(3\times 1\).

selfCheck.prompt: How does adding a ridge penalty \(\lambda ||w||^{2}/2\) change the Hessian?
selfCheck.answer: H becomes \(XX^\mathrm{T}+\lambda I\). Every eigenvalue increases by \(\lambda\), stabilizing the inverse, but the estimate is biased toward zero; regularization must not be mistaken for additional data.

pitfalls: Treating existence of a closed-form inverse as proof that the biological parameters are unique.
Ignoring feature scaling; different units directly alter Hessian eigenvalues and comparisons of stiffness.

modules.title: The Hessian eigenbasis, stiff/sloppy directions, and model ensembles
modules.guidingQuestion: Why can many individual weights vary widely while the data tightly constrain a few parameter combinations?
paragraphs: A Hessian is symmetric positive-semidefinite, so \(H=VDV^\mathrm{T}\), where columns \(v_{k}\) are orthonormal parameter directions and D contains \(\lambda _{k}\ge 0\). Let \(z=V^\mathrm{T}(w-\hat{w})\); then the quadratic loss increase is \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\). A large \(\lambda _{k}\) gives a large loss for the same displacement and defines a stiff direction. A small \(\lambda _{k}\) permits farther movement within the adequate-fit contour and defines a sloppy direction.

The fit shown on the source page has about 4 stiff and 46 sloppy dimensions. Those counts belong to that model, dataset, and parameterization; they are not universal constants of oculomotor circuits. In a two-direction example, the error contour is an elongated ellipse: its short axis corresponds to large \(\lambda\) and its long axis to small \(\lambda\). Each axis is generally a mixture of many weights, so calling one parameter sloppy is often imprecise.

Sloppiness can reflect genuine functional compensation, but also failure of an experiment to excite certain modes, large measurement noise, collinear features, or poor parameter scaling. It does not make the associated biology irrelevant. A direction that is sloppy for the current eye-position dataset may matter during perturbation, development, or another behavior. New conditions are needed to distinguish biological degeneracy from insufficient data.

Reporting one best-fit W hides this structure. Instead, collect all models with loss below a prespecified adequacy threshold, compare their common predictions, and identify experiments on which they disagree most. A perturbation outcome predicted by every model is robust; divergence along a sloppy valley identifies an experiment that can narrow the ensemble. Sloppiness in parameter space is distinct from low dimensionality of neural states in Lecture19.
keyPoints: \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\) decomposes curvature along parameter eigen-directions.
Large \(\lambda\) is stiff; small \(\lambda\) is sloppy.
A sloppy direction usually combines multiple parameters and does not mean that one synapse is irrelevant.
An adequate-model ensemble expresses uncertainty and robust predictions better than a single best fit.

derivation.title: Derive ellipse-axis lengths from curvature
derivation.setup: In a two-dimensional Hessian eigenbasis, fix the allowable loss increase and find how far one may move along each direction.

steps.title: Diagonalize H
steps.explanation: Use \(z=V^\mathrm{T}\Delta w\) to eliminate cross terms.

steps.title: Set the adequacy threshold
steps.explanation: Let \(\Delta L\le c\); the boundary is \(\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}=2c\).

steps.title: Find an axis radius
steps.explanation: Along axis k, set all other coordinates to 0.

steps.title: Compare stiff and sloppy
steps.explanation: Radius is proportional to \(1/\sqrt \lambda\); an eigenvalue ratio of 10000 gives an axis-length ratio of 100.

symbolNotes: \(z_{k}\) uses parameter units after rotation by V; if the original parameters have different units, scale them sensibly first.
c is the permitted loss increase; its statistical interpretation depends on the noise model.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\lambda _{k}\) has units of loss/\(parameter^{2}\), so taking the square root of \(2c/\lambda _{k}\) restores parameter units.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\lambda _{k}=0\), the quadratic approximation gives an infinitely flat direction, meaning that the data do not constrain that combination at all. Actual bounds or higher-order terms may truncate it.

workedExample.title: Compare two curvature directions
workedExample.problem: The Hessian eigenvalues are 100 and 0.01, and the allowed \(\Delta L\) is 0.5. Find the maximum displacement along each axis and their ratio.
steps: \(2c=1\). The stiff radius is \(\sqrt{1/100}=0.1\).
The sloppy radius is \(\sqrt{1/0.01}=10\).
The ratio is \(10/0.1=100\); at the same loss tolerance, the sloppy direction permits a displacement 100 times larger.
workedExample.result: The adequate-fit ellipse is extremely long along the small-eigenvalue direction, directly visualizing parameter compensation or weak constraint.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The eigenvalue ratio is \(100/0.01=10000\), so the axis ratio is its square root, 100, not 10000.

selfCheck.prompt: Why can sloppy not be translated as 'this parameter is unimportant'?
selfCheck.answer: A Hessian direction usually combines parameters, and small curvature means only that the current data and loss are insensitive to it. The combination may still be crucial for an unmeasured behavior, a perturbation response, or biological viability.

pitfalls: Comparing Hessian eigenvalues of unstandardized parameters and creating artificial sloppiness through unit differences.
Interchanging parameter-space Hessian eigenvectors with neural-activity PCs or dynamical modes.

objectives: Distinguish three levels of description—single-neuron directional tuning, low-dimensional population trajectories, and latent dynamics—and explain how all three can hold simultaneously.
Explain each component of GPFA from high-dimensional neural activity to low-dimensional factors, including the observation model, temporal covariance, matrix shapes, and non-identifiability.
Use a delayed-reach timeline to explain how preparatory states enter movement-potent and output-null subspaces without misrepresenting graphical correlations as causal conclusions.
Compute the null space and rank–nullity of a linear readout by hand, construct a simple decoder, and apply the results to closed-loop BMI and cross-day alignment.
Connect PCA/GPFA, linear readout, closed-loop feedback, and cross-day alignment into a testable BMI analysis pipeline.
prerequisiteBridge: Represent one population recording as a vector. If N neurons are recorded simultaneously, their firing rates at one moment form an N-dimensional vector r. Each plotted point is not a neuron; it is the state of the entire population at that moment. PCA or a factor model describes those points with K coordinates, where K is smaller than N. Low dimensionality does not mean that only a few neurons were recorded; it means that the variation of many neurons is constrained by a few shared variables.

Interpret the linear map \(C\alpha +d\) as a multidimensional shadow. \(\alpha\) is a K-dimensional latent coordinate, each column of C specifies the activity pattern that one latent factor leaves across N neurons, and d is the mean offset. The shapes must be C: N×K, \(\alpha\): K×1, and output: N×1. Adding \(\Sigma\) acknowledges trial noise and unmodeled fluctuations even for the same latent state.

A Gaussian process does not mean that activity has a Gaussian-shaped profile. It assigns a joint distribution to a time-varying latent function at every pair of times. The kernel \(K(t,t')\) sets how long separated points remain similar. In a squared-exponential kernel, \(\tau\) is the smoothing time scale; larger \(\tau\) makes the latent trajectory vary more slowly. This distinction lets us discuss smooth trajectories, preparatory states, linear readouts, and closed-loop decoders separately.

diagnostic.prompt: If 100 neurons are recorded and 6 latent factors are retained, what is the shape of the GPFA loading matrix C?
diagnostic.answer: C is \(100\times 6\); it maps a \(6\times 1\) latent vector to a \(100\times 1\) mean neural-activity vector.
diagnostic.explanation: Check matrix multiplication from output dimension back to input dimension; do not mix trials or time bins into the neuron axis of C.

diagnostic.prompt: Does a directional tuning curve prove that the neuron directly encodes force in one muscle?
diagnostic.answer: No. Tuning establishes a statistical association between firing rate and reach direction; it may arise from input, shared dynamics, task covariates, or a readout.
diagnostic.explanation: A causal encoding claim additionally requires control of confounders and tests of perturbations and decoder generalization.

diagnostic.prompt: If U is \(2\times 5\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(U)=2\), what is the dimension of its linear output-null space?
diagnostic.answer: By rank–nullity, the dimension is \(5-2=3\).
diagnostic.explanation: Null-space dimension is input dimension minus rank, not output dimension minus rank.

diagnostic.prompt: As \(\tau\) in a GP kernel increases, do neighboring latent values usually become smoother or more abrupt?
diagnostic.answer: Smoother. A fixed temporal separation becomes smaller relative to \(\tau\), making kernel covariance closer to its maximum.
diagnostic.explanation: Substitute both limits into the kernel: with very large \(\tau\), the exponential approaches 1; with very small \(\tau\), covariance at a nonzero lag falls rapidly.

diagnostic.prompt: Why should a cross-day decoder not require exact correspondence of individual neuron identities every day?
diagnostic.answer: Electrode drift changes which units are visible. If the stable computation lies in a latent subspace, align each day's latent coordinates before decoding.
diagnostic.explanation: Cross-day stability is a hypothesis about population structure. It must be tested on held-out days and cannot be confirmed by an attractive two-dimensional plot.

modules.title: Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories
modules.guidingQuestion: Why can the same center-out data support directional tuning curves and also be viewed as projections of a low-dimensional dynamical system?
paragraphs: A center-out task begins at a central location and reaches toward multiple radial targets, making direction, speed, and time from the go cue well structured. For one neuron, mean directional tuning can be described by \(r(\theta )=b+k \cos(\theta -\theta _{\mathrm{pref}})\), where \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) is preferred direction and k is modulation depth. This formula summarizes a condition average; it does not mean the neuron 'knows' the angle or guarantee that other movement variables have been excluded.

Stack all neuronal rates at one moment into \(r(t)\), so each reach condition traces an N-dimensional trajectory. If most variance lies on a few PCs, the trajectory is close to a low-dimensional subspace. A single-neuron curve is the shadow of the high-dimensional trajectory on one coordinate axis. Multiple phase-shifted shadows can arise from one rotating or curved population trajectory, so tuning and dynamics are compatible observations.

PCA orders dimensions by variance; it does not know which dimension drives muscles. A low-variance dimension may carry a small but behaviorally crucial output, especially if the readout has high gain along it. Conversely, a large-variance dimension may be output-null preparation. Judging usefulness requires both neural covariance and the behavioral readout, not explained variance alone.

The two-dimensional loops or clusters in teaching figures are projections. Overlap may result from truncation, while separation may be exaggerated by normalization. Record the time axis, condition colors, whether trials were averaged, and whether PCs were fitted jointly across conditions. If PCA is fitted separately per condition, the trajectories no longer share coordinates and cannot be compared for target-specific preparation.
keyPoints: Directional tuning is a statistical condition average, not a unique neural code.
Single-cell tuning can be a coordinate projection of a low-dimensional population trajectory.
PCA variance and motor potency are different criteria.

derivation.title: Directional tuning as a linear projection of a two-dimensional movement vector
derivation.setup: Write a two-dimensional reach direction as a unit vector and let the neuron respond linearly to its two coordinates.

steps.title: Write the direction vector
steps.explanation: The unit movement vector at angle \(\theta\) has horizontal and vertical components.

steps.title: Write the sensitivity direction
steps.explanation: Express preferred direction as a unit vector too, with modulation gain k.

steps.title: Compute the dot product
steps.explanation: Apply the cosine angle-difference identity to obtain the tuning curve.

symbolNotes: r and b are in Hz; k is a modulation amplitude in Hz.
\(\theta\) and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) must use the same angular unit and are conventionally treated as radians inside trigonometric functions.
derivation.unitsCheck: The direction vectors in the dot product are dimensionless; multiplying by k yields Hz, which can be added to baseline b.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(k=0\), every direction gives b. At \(\theta =\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) the rate is b+k, and in the opposite direction it is b-k.

workedExample.title: Compute tuning at four directions
workedExample.problem: A neuron has \(b=20 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(k=8 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}=0\). Find the predicted rates at \(\theta =0\), \(\pi /2\), \(\pi\), and \(3\pi /2\).
steps: At \(\theta =0\), \(\cos 0=1\), giving 28 Hz.
At \(\pi /2\) and \(3\pi /2\), the cosine is 0, giving 20 Hz in both cases.
At \(\pi\), cos\(\pi =-1\), giving 12 Hz.
workedExample.result: The four rates are 28, 20, 12, and 20 Hz, respectively.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The maximum and minimum are symmetric around the 20 Hz baseline, and their mean remains 20 Hz.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does a PC explaining 70% of neural variance not necessarily explain 70% of behavioral variance?
selfCheck.answer: Behavior depends on a separate readout map, which may ignore high-variance directions or amplify low-variance directions; there is no fixed ratio between the two variances.

pitfalls: Treating a cosine-fit preferred direction as an immutable causal label.
Mistaking the smoothness of a trial-averaged projection for noise-free single trials.

modules.title: Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model
modules.guidingQuestion: How does GPFA map a few smooth latent functions into many neurons, and what does each matrix dimension represent?
paragraphs: Let \(r_{t}\) be the observed vector from N neurons in time bin t and \(\alpha _{t}\) contain K latent factors. Conditional on \(\alpha _{t}\), \(r_{t}\) follows a multivariate Gaussian with \(\operatorname{mean} C\alpha _{t}+d\) and covariance \(\Sigma\). Rows of C correspond to neurons, columns to factors, and d is each neuron's baseline. For spike counts, the Gaussian is an approximation; with very narrow bins or low rates, a Poisson observation model may be more appropriate.

A K-dimensional trajectory in latent space is embedded by C into N-dimensional activity space. The column span of C is the shared-activity subspace allowed by the model, while \(\Sigma\) usually absorbs neuron-specific residuals. Shared variation does not require neuron pairs to have identical waveforms: positive and negative loadings allow one factor to produce different amplitudes and directions across cells.

The conditional observation mean has a coordinate reparameterization. For any invertible K×K matrix A, define \(\alpha '=A\alpha\) and \(C'=CA^{-1}\); then \(C'\alpha '=C\alpha\). This proves only that the conditional mean is unchanged. Preserving the full GPFA marginal likelihood also requires transforming the latent prior covariance to \(A K A^\mathrm{T}\). Standard GPFA usually assumes independent factors that may have different temporal kernels; arbitrary rotation generally introduces between-factor covariance and leaves that model family. Sign flips, factor permutations, and paired scale changes are common ambiguities. More general rotational equivalence requires extra conditions such as identical kernels or an allowed correlated prior.

The GP prior supplies the temporal structure of \(\alpha\), while the observation model supplies the spatial relationship between r and \(\alpha\). Their roles cannot be reversed: C does not smooth time, and the kernel does not specify each neuron's loading. If \(\Sigma\) is diagonal, residual neurons are conditionally independent given the latent state. Strong remaining residual correlations may indicate too few factors K, a poor kernel, or an oversimplified noise model.
keyPoints: C is N×K and links latent space with neural activity space.
\(\Sigma\) describes residuals conditional on the latent state; it is not the covariance of the raw data.
Conditional observation coordinates can be reparameterized; equivalence of the full GPFA also depends on the latent prior.

derivation.title: Shapes in the observation model and reparameterizing its conditional mean
derivation.setup: Check every vector shape, then prove that latent reparameterization leaves the conditional mean unchanged. This alone does not prove that the full GP prior or marginal likelihood is unchanged.

steps.title: List the shapes
steps.explanation: With N neurons and K factors, the matrix product must have N outputs.
steps.latex: C\in\mathbb R^{N\times K},\quad\boldsymbol\alpha_t\in\mathbb R^K,\quad\mathbf d\in\mathbb R^N

steps.title: Write the conditional mean
steps.explanation: The center of the observation Gaussian lies in activity space.

steps.title: Apply an invertible transformation
steps.explanation: Define the new latent coordinates as \(A\alpha\) and change the loading inversely.

steps.title: Verify unchanged predictions
steps.explanation: Multiplication cancels \(A^{-1}A\), so both coordinate systems give the same conditional mean. The transformed prior covariance must still be checked separately for the full model.

symbolNotes: N is the number of neurons and K is latent dimensionality, usually with \(K<N\).
\(\Sigma\) is an N×N covariance whose diagonal entries are residual variances. After transformation by A, a latent prior covariance generally no longer retains a factor-wise diagonal structure.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(C\alpha\) and d must share the units of r. If \(\alpha\) is dimensionless, entries of C have units of rate or count. \(\Sigma\) uses squared observation units.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(K=N\) and C is invertible, there is no dimensionality reduction. If all latent factors share an identical kernel, an orthogonal rotation can preserve the prior form; different kernels generally preclude arbitrary rotation.

workedExample.title: Reconstruct two neurons from one factor
workedExample.problem: Let \(C=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), \(d=(10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\alpha =3\) at one moment. Find the predicted rates.
steps: The first neuron's mean is \(2\times 3+10=16 \mathrm{Hz}\).
The second neuron's mean is \(-1\times 3+20=17 \mathrm{Hz}\).
A negative loading means that as the latent increases, the second neuron falls below baseline; it does not imply a negative firing rate.
workedExample.result: The predicted mean is \((16,17)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: Setting \(\alpha\) to 0 should recover the baseline \((10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\).

selfCheck.prompt: If one latent factor is multiplied everywhere by 2 without changing C, is it still the same GPFA model?
selfCheck.answer: No; the predicted mean changes. It is an equivalent coordinate reparameterization only if the corresponding column of C is also divided by 2.

pitfalls: Treating a latent factor as a directly measured neuron.
Concluding from diagonal \(\Sigma\) that real neurons are independent; independence applies only to residuals conditional on the latent state.

modules.title: GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories
modules.guidingQuestion: How does a squared-exponential kernel encode smoothness, and how should target preparation, go cue, and movement be separated in delayed reaches?
paragraphs: The squared-exponential kernel \(K(t,t')=\sigma s^{2}\) \(\exp[-(t-t')^{2}/(2\tau ^{2})]+\sigma n^{2}\delta tt'\) gives covariance between two times for one factor. \(\sigma s^{2}\) controls smooth signal variance, \(\tau\) controls the correlation-decay time, and \(\sigma n^{2}\) adds independent variability only in the same time bin. The original Page 3 notes a global scale ambiguity between \(\alpha\) and loading C and uses \(\sigma n^{2}+\sigma s^{2}=1\) as a normalization convention. That constraint fixes scale; it is not a new biological law. Nor is this the only GP kernel: for rapid switching or oscillation, Matérn or periodic kernels may better match the hypothesis.

Fitting jointly estimates latent trajectories, loadings, baselines, noise, and kernel hyperparameters, commonly by marginal likelihood or an EM-like procedure. Increasing K always increases in-sample flexibility, so choose dimensionality with cross-validation, held-out likelihood, or reconstruction prediction. Training explained variance alone can mistake noise dimensions for meaningful factors.

Read a delayed-reach plot along its timeline. The interval after target onset but before the go cue is the preparatory epoch; movement begins only after go. Preparatory activity for different targets may approach different latent locations without producing obvious movement. After the cue, trajectories depart from those initial states along target-specific movement paths. The plot supports the idea that an initial condition influences later dynamics, but trajectories alone cannot exclude sustained common input.

Trial averaging clarifies preparatory trajectories but conceals single-trial onset jitter and variability. To claim that trajectory geometry predicts behavior, use the pre-go latent state to predict reaction time, directional error, or muscle activity on held-out trials. A post-go divergence may reflect alignment and condition averaging, so compare it with shuffled labels and alternative alignments.
keyPoints: \(\tau\) is a temporal correlation scale, not trial duration.
A kernel family is a modeling assumption that must be tested with held-out data.
Target, go, and movement events must delimit the epochs of a delayed-reach trajectory.

derivation.title: Two limits of the squared-exponential kernel
derivation.setup: Fix the time difference \(\Delta t\) and compare covariance when \(\tau\) is much larger or much smaller than that difference.

steps.title: Rewrite the time difference
steps.explanation: Let \(\Delta t=t-t'\) and first consider distinct time bins, for which the Kronecker delta is zero.

steps.title: Take the long-time-scale limit
steps.explanation: When \(\tau\) is much larger than \(|\Delta t|\), the exponent is close to zero.

steps.title: Take the short-time-scale limit
steps.explanation: For fixed nonzero \(\Delta t\), the exponent approaches negative infinity as \(\tau\) approaches zero.

steps.title: Add same-bin noise
steps.explanation: At \(t=t'\), signal variance and diagonal noise variance add.

symbolNotes: \(\sigma s^{2}\) and \(\sigma n^{2}\) have squared latent-amplitude units. The source page fixes this factor's arbitrary global scale with \(\sigma n^{2}+\sigma s^{2}=1\).
\(\tau\) and t use the same time unit; \(\delta tt'\) is a discrete time-bin indicator.
derivation.unitsCheck: The numerator and denominator of the exponent both have units of time squared, so their ratio is dimensionless; K retains units of latent variance.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\tau \to \infty\), the factor is nearly constant within a finite window. As \(\tau \to 0\), between-bin covariance vanishes and the smooth prior degenerates.

workedExample.title: Compare correlation strength at two time lags
workedExample.problem: Ignore \(\sigma n\) and set \(\sigma s^{2}=1\) and \(\tau =100 \mathrm{ms}\). Approximate the covariance for \(\Delta t=100 \mathrm{ms}\) and 200 ms.
steps: At \(\Delta t=100\), the exponent is -1/2 and \(K=e^{-1/2}\approx 0.607\).
At \(\Delta t=200\), the exponent is \(-4/2=-2\) and \(K=e^{-2}\approx 0.135\).
The second lag is twice as long, but covariance falls by more than a factor of four because distance is squared.
workedExample.result: The two values are approximately 0.607 and 0.135.
workedExample.sanityCheck: At \(\Delta t=0\) the value should be 1; the kernel decreases monotonically as \(|\Delta t|\) grows.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does a smooth kernel not prove that the true cortical trajectory is intrinsically smooth?
selfCheck.answer: Some smoothness comes from the prior. Compare held-out data, alternative kernels, and temporal resolutions to determine whether the data support that time scale.

pitfalls: Mistaking \(\tau\) for the number K of latent factors.
Interpreting divergence after the go cue as recurrent causality without testing a sustained-input model.

modules.title: Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space
modules.guidingQuestion: How can a linear readout produce zero motor output despite strong neural activity during preparation?
paragraphs: Write a locally linear readout as \(m=Ur\), where r is an N-dimensional neural state and m an M-dimensional motor command; U must therefore be M×N. The original Page 4 labels U as N×M, which is incompatible with \(m=Ur\), so we correct it to M×N. Any nonzero r satisfying \(Ur=0\) lies in the null space of U; the neurons need not be silent. Preparatory activity can move the network along null directions without changing output in this approximation. After the go cue, the state enters potent directions and the readout becomes nonzero.

Rank–nullity gives dim Null\((U)=N-\operatorname{rank}(U)\). This simplifies to the source page's N-M only when U has full row \(\operatorname{rank} M\); if \(\operatorname{rank}(U)<M\), the null space is larger. When recording dimension greatly exceeds motor-output dimension, a large null space is theoretically possible. But recorded r samples only some neurons, and the true downstream map may be nonlinear, state-dependent, or delayed. The null space of a fitted U is therefore relative to a model, not an anatomically absolute no-output pathway.

Use the singular value decomposition of U to write r=rpotent+rnull. Row-space directions change output, while their orthogonal complement belongs to the null space. Test whether preparatory activity is output-null by fitting U on independent trials, measuring pre-go projections, and checking EMG or kinematics. Choosing a direction and reporting zero output on the same data is circular.

Output-null does not mean computation-null. Activity along a null direction can set a recurrent initial condition, suppress an erroneous movement, or prepare multiple candidates. The same neural vector may also affect unrecorded downstream populations. The course diagram is a linear framework that separates the existence of activity from the existence of current output; it does not justify calling null activity biologically functionless.
keyPoints: \(Ur=0\) can hold with \(r\ne 0\).
Null-space size is determined by input dimensionality and rank.
Output-null is a model statement relative to a specified readout U.

derivation.title: Rank–nullity and the potent/null decomposition
derivation.setup: For an M×N readout U, use linear algebra to show how a nonzero preparatory state can produce no output.

steps.title: Write the readout
steps.explanation: The output is a linear combination of the neural state.

steps.title: Define the null space
steps.explanation: All input vectors mapped to zero form a linear subspace.

steps.title: Compute its dimension
steps.explanation: Rank–nullity makes visible output directions and invisible input directions sum to N.

steps.title: Verify the decomposition
steps.explanation: If rnull is in the null space, it does not change the output determined by the potent component.

symbolNotes: M is the number of output coordinates, and N is the number of neural coordinates.
\(\operatorname{rank}(U)\) cannot exceed \(\min(M,N)\); all vectors must use the same centering convention.
derivation.unitsCheck: If r is in Hz and m in command units, U has units of command units/Hz; the zero vector carries the corresponding output units.
derivation.limitCheck: If U has full column rank and \(N\le M\), its null space contains only the zero vector. If N≫M, the null space has at least N-M dimensions.

workedExample.title: Compute an output-null vector
workedExample.problem: Let \(U=[1,2]\) and \(r=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Find m and give one potent vector.
steps: \(m=1\times 2+2\times (-1)=0\), so r is a nonzero null vector.
Choose rpotent=\((1,0)^\mathrm{T}\), giving \(m=1\).
Adding the two vectors gives \((3,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), whose output remains \(3+2\times (-1)=1\).
workedExample.result: The null component changes the neural state without changing the original potent output of 1.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A null vector of U has zero dot product with the row vector (1,2), so the two are geometrically orthogonal.

selfCheck.prompt: If the downstream readout changes to \(U'\), must the original output-null vector remain null?
selfCheck.answer: No. The null space depends on the particular readout. One neural direction may be irrelevant to one output yet affect another muscle group or cognitive variable.

pitfalls: Incorrectly inferring \(r=0\) from \(Ur=0\).
Defining and testing the null space on the same training trials, thereby overfitting.

modules.title: Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment
modules.guidingQuestion: When recorded units change from day to day, how can closed-loop feedback and latent alignment keep a decoder working?
paragraphs: A BMI decoder maps neural features to cursor velocity, position, or a discrete action. During open-loop calibration, the participant observes prescribed movement or attempts an action while the system fits a mapping offline. In closed loop, decoder output immediately changes visual feedback, so participant and decoder coadapt. Closed-loop performance is therefore not a passive measure of a fixed encoding; the brain, decoder, and feedback form a new dynamical system.

Suppose the observation on day d is \(r_{d}=C_{d}\alpha +d_{d}+\mathrm{noise}\). Different electrode samples change \(C_{d}\) while similar latent dynamics may persist. A cross-day method first estimates daily subspaces and then finds \(A_{d}\) to make their \(\alpha\) coordinates comparable; it finally applies \(\hat{v}=B\alpha\) in the aligned latent space. Stability here means that a transferable low-dimensional relationship exists, not that each neuron's loading is constant.

Alignment can manufacture false stability. If behavior labels from the current day rotate latent space and the decoder is then tested on that same day, the answer has leaked into the analysis. A strict evaluation uses calibration data alone to estimate \(A_{d}\) and B, tests on held-out blocks or future days, compares no alignment, random alignment, and a direct neuron-space decoder, and reports adaptation time and failure days.

These concepts form one closed loop: PCA/GPFA supplies a shared subspace, a linear readout supplies the behavioral map, closed-loop feedback changes the data distribution, and alignment handles coordinate drift. Every step has assumptions; 'stable latent structure' must not be expanded into permanent invariance of single-neuron representations.
keyPoints: A closed-loop BMI is a joint brain–decoder–feedback system.
Cross-day alignment aligns population coordinates rather than demanding stable unit identity.
Holding out future days prevents behavior labels from leaking into the alignment result.

derivation.title: Mapping chain of a cross-day latent decoder
derivation.setup: Project each day's observation into a within-day latent space, align it to reference coordinates, and then decode.

steps.title: Write the daily observation
steps.explanation: Changes in electrode sampling appear in the daily loading and baseline.

steps.title: Align the coordinates
steps.explanation: Use \(A_{d}\) to map day d's latent coordinate into the reference latent space.

steps.title: Apply the shared decoder
steps.explanation: Use the same B for behavioral prediction in aligned coordinates.

steps.title: Define held-out error
steps.explanation: Compare true and predicted velocity on time bins used in neither alignment nor fitting.

symbolNotes: \(C_{d}\) is neurons×latents, \(A_{d}\) is latents×latents, and B is outputs×latents.
The number of neurons may vary across days, but aligned latent dimensionality must be constant.
derivation.unitsCheck: If velocity is in cm/s and the latent is dimensionless, B is in cm/s; squared error is in \(\mathrm{cm}^{2}/s^{2}\).
derivation.limitCheck: \(A_{d}=I\) means that no rotation is required. If latent subspaces do not overlap at all, linear alignment should not be expected to recover an accurate decoder.

workedExample.title: Swap the axes of a two-dimensional latent space
workedExample.problem: On day 2, latent coordinates are swapped relative to day 1: \(\alpha _{2}=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\), whereas the reference order is \((1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Give the alignment and compute the prediction for \(B=[2,-1]\).
steps: Use \(A=[[0,1],[1,0]]\) to swap the coordinates, giving \(\widetilde{\alpha }=(1,3)^\mathrm{T}\).
Apply B: \(\hat{v}=2\times 1-1\times 3=-1\).
Without alignment, the result is \(2\times 3-1\times 1=5\), showing how a coordinate-convention change can seriously disrupt the decoder.
workedExample.result: The aligned prediction is -1; the unaligned prediction is 5.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A is a permutation matrix, so \(A^\mathrm{T} A=I\) and latent-vector length is unchanged.

selfCheck.prompt: Why can an improvement in closed-loop performance not be attributed entirely to more accurate decoder parameters?
selfCheck.answer: The participant changes neural strategy in response to feedback, and the decoder may update online. Performance comes from joint adaptation, so one side must be frozen or otherwise controlled to separate the causes.

pitfalls: Treating aligned latent stability as permanent stability of individual-neuron identity.
Using test-day behavior to choose an alignment and then reporting those same data as cross-day generalization.

objectives: Organize decision-making, working memory, and long-term learning around the working definition that current brain state is not determined solely by current input, while recognizing that this is not an exhaustive definition.
Reconstruct DMS and Romo parametric working-memory tasks through sample, delay, comparison, and choice, specifying what information must be retained during the delay.
Derive the effective time constant of graded persistent activity from a recurrent eigenmode and classify leaky, perfectly persistent, and unstable regimes.
Explain the evidence, noise, bias, bounds, and reaction time of a leaky drift-diffusion process, and predict its psychometric and chronometric curves.
Use the Wong–Wang phase plane to distinguish fixed points, separatrices, and stochastic choice while keeping model predictions separate from correlations in LIP.
prerequisiteBridge: A short-term memory problem can begin with a minimal state equation. After the external sample disappears, an internal variable x must retain a sample-dependent value. If \(dx/dt=0\), the value persists; if \(dx/dt=-x/\tau\), it decays exponentially. When feedback cancels leak, the effective \(\tau\) can greatly exceed a single cell's membrane time constant. Intuition about exponentials and first-order differential equations is enough to begin; the derivation below places a recurrent eigenvalue inside this decay rate.

Decision-making instead accumulates noisy evidence over time into a variable a. Positive evidence pushes toward the right option and negative evidence toward the left; choice occurs when a first hits +B or -B. Each trial has a different noise realization, so the same stimulus strength yields probabilistic choices and a distribution of reaction times. Keep distinct the effects of drift on mean direction, noise on dispersion, initial bias on starting point, and bound height on the speed–accuracy tradeoff.

A phase plane plots two state variables together. Each nullcline makes only one derivative zero; their intersection is a fixed point. Nearby arrows determine stability, and a separatrix divides initial states that flow to different attractors. This geometry connects the bound rule of a one-dimensional accumulator to nonlinear recurrent choice attractors, but the two are different models.

diagnostic.prompt: DMS needs only a memory that the sample was seen. What additional information must the Romo task preserve?
diagnostic.answer: The Romo parametric task must retain the continuous or graded value of the first vibration frequency so it can be compared with the second.
diagnostic.explanation: A one-bit 'sample occurred' label cannot explain graded comparison errors between nearby frequencies.

diagnostic.prompt: For a recurrent mode with \(\lambda =0.9\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), what is the effective time constant?
diagnostic.answer: \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.9)=200 \mathrm{ms}\).
diagnostic.explanation: First compute the eigenvalue gap \(1-\lambda\), then divide the intrinsic time constant by it; \(\lambda\) has no time units.

diagnostic.prompt: If only decision bound B is increased, how do accuracy and reaction time usually change in a DDM?
diagnostic.answer: With other parameters fixed and informative trials, accuracy usually increases and reaction time lengthens.
diagnostic.explanation: A farther bound permits more evidence collection but requires a longer first-passage time.

diagnostic.prompt: Both LIP firing rate and the model decision variable ramp. Is that enough to conclude that LIP implements a DDM?
diagnostic.answer: No. Similar temporal shapes are correlational and can arise from common input, urgency, condition averaging, or other dynamics.
diagnostic.explanation: The claim additionally requires trial-level covariation, perturbations, parameter-linked predictions, and comparison with alternative models.

diagnostic.prompt: What happens when a phase-plane trajectory lies exactly on a separatrix?
diagnostic.answer: In an ideal deterministic system it follows the boundary toward a saddle; a minute noise fluctuation or bias pushes it into one of the two choice basins.
diagnostic.explanation: A separatrix is not a broad third choice region; it is the boundary between attractor basins.

modules.title: A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input
modules.guidingQuestion: How can the course's definition of cognition become a testable state dependence rather than an abstract label?
paragraphs: This lecture adopts a working definition: cognition makes brain state or behavior incompletely determined by present sensory input. The same current stimulus can produce different responses under different memories, goals, or beliefs; conversely, an internal decision variable can keep evolving while the outside world is unchanged. This definition is useful for modeling, but it is not a complete philosophical definition of consciousness, language, or intelligence.

A test presents the same current input after different histories. If sample identity, previous reward, or instruction changes delay activity and choice, the system requires a history-dependent state. Control current stimulus, movement preparation, and arousal; otherwise an apparent internal state may simply be an omitted external or bodily variable.

Decision-making, short-term memory, learning, and generalization operate on different time scales but can all be written as state updates. A decision state accumulates evidence over hundreds of milliseconds; working memory retains a sample for a delay of seconds; learning changes parameters across trials; long-term memory retrieves information over much longer intervals. A shared mathematical language does not imply a shared brain area or cellular mechanism.

Use a Markov-state question while learning: if present input alone does not predict the next event, which added internal variable improves prediction? The variable may be accumulated evidence, a remembered frequency, or a task rule. A good model explains how state is written, maintained without input, read, and cleared; it does more than draw a high firing trace during a delay.
keyPoints: The working definition emphasizes a history-dependent internal state.
The key experimental control holds current input fixed while varying the past.
A shared state-space language does not imply a shared biological mechanism.

derivation.title: Express 'current input is insufficient' with conditional probability
derivation.setup: Compare choice predictions conditioned only on current stimulus with predictions conditioned additionally on history.

steps.title: Define the current-input model
steps.explanation: If current input \(X_{t}\) is sufficient, past history \(H_{t}\) should not further change the choice distribution.

steps.title: Introduce an internal state
steps.explanation: Use state \(Z_{t}\) to compress task-relevant history.

steps.title: Construct the test
steps.explanation: Hold \(X_{t}\) fixed and compare choices across different \(Z_{t}\) values or history conditions.

symbolNotes: \(X_{t}\) is current observable input, \(H_{t}\) is past events, and \(Z_{t}\) is internal state.
\(Y_{t}\) may be choice, reaction time, or a neural response.
derivation.unitsCheck: These are probabilities, dimensionless and between 0 and 1; the conditioning variables themselves may have different units.
derivation.limitCheck: If a history effect vanishes after all observable current inputs are included, no additional cognitive state is needed to explain that effect.

workedExample.title: Identify history dependence
workedExample.problem: Two trial groups share a current comparison stimulus of 20 Hz. The first sample is 10 Hz in one group and 30 Hz in the other. Animals predominantly choose 'comparison larger' and 'comparison smaller,' respectively.
steps: Because the current comparison is identical, a current-input-only model predicts the same choice distribution.
Different sample histories change both the correct relation and actual choice.
The internal state must carry at least the sample's relation to 20 Hz to explain the difference.
workedExample.result: This design supports a history-dependent state, but recording or intervention is still needed to identify its particular neural code.
workedExample.sanityCheck: First rule out confounds if motor cues or rewards also differ systematically between the groups.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does continued brain activity with the eyes closed not by itself prove cognition in this lecture's sense?
selfCheck.answer: Persistent activity may be spontaneous fluctuation or an unmeasured input. It must carry task-relevant history and predict later behavior.

pitfalls: Treating a working definition as the only definition of cognition.
Failing to measure eye movements or body state and misattributing their effects to internal memory.

modules.title: Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory
modules.guidingQuestion: After the sample disappears, must memory preserve only a categorical label or a continuously comparable quantity?
paragraphs: Delayed match-to-sample presents a sample, a delay, and a test in order, followed by a match or nonmatch report. The minimum memory content may be sample identity or category. Because no sample is directly available during the delay, above-chance behavior shows that past information remains accessible. The strategy could nevertheless use a verbal label, familiarity, or a rule-specific code and does not automatically imply an exact sensory trace.

In the Romo vibration task, frequency f1 is delivered to a fingertip, followed after a delay by f2; the animal judges whether f2 is greater or less than f1. Comparing neighboring frequencies requires a graded magnitude, not merely a 'stimulus occurred' marker. If the delay representation is noisy, f1 and f2 become harder to discriminate as they approach each other, and psychometric slope can estimate their combined sensory and memory uncertainty.

Align neural data to each event. The sample epoch tests encoding; the delay tests maintenance; the comparison epoch asks how remembered f1 and current f2 combine into a decision variable; and the choice epoch also contains motor preparation. A cell whose delay firing is ordered by f1 is a candidate memory signal, but trial-to-trial fluctuations should predict comparison errors rather than relying only on condition means.

DMS and parametric memory differ chiefly in readout demands. A DMS classifier may only need to separate finitely many patterns, whereas a Romo comparison must preserve ordering and distance. Poor performance cannot be assigned directly to maintenance failure; it may arise in sample encoding, comparison sensation, the decision rule, or motor report. Perturbations must be restricted to a particular epoch to separate these stages.
keyPoints: DMS can be supported by categorical or identity memory.
The Romo task must preserve a comparable magnitude for f1.
Epoch-specific recording and perturbation separate encoding, maintenance, and readout.

workedExample.title: Make a comparison from noisy memory
workedExample.problem: The internal memory value is \(m_{1}=18 \mathrm{Hz}\), the comparison estimate is \(m_{2}=22 \mathrm{Hz}\), and the rule is to choose 'second is larger' when \(m_{2}-m_{1}>0\). Ignoring decision noise, find the choice variable.
steps: Compute \(d=m_{2}-m_{1}=22-18=4 \mathrm{Hz}\).
Since \(d>0\), the result lies on the 'second is larger' side.
If memory error overestimates m1 beyond 22 Hz, the choice reverses, showing that an error need not arise from comparison sensation.
workedExample.result: The decision variable is +4 Hz, predicting the choice 'second is larger.'
workedExample.sanityCheck: Swapping the two estimates should produce -4 Hz and the opposite choice.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does monotonic delay-period firing with f1 not by itself prove that this is the memory used for behavior?
selfCheck.answer: The correlated signal could be a passive readout. Functional evidence is stronger when its trial fluctuations, selective perturbation, or downstream coupling affect comparison behavior.

pitfalls: Attributing every drop in accuracy to forgetting without checking other task epochs.
Extending a mechanism for discrete DMS directly to continuous frequency memory.

modules.title: Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one
modules.guidingQuestion: How can recurrent feedback maintain a population mode for seconds when individual neurons have time constants of only tens of milliseconds?
paragraphs: Linearized population dynamics can be written \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\). Project activity onto an eigenvector v of W. If \(Wv=\lambda v\), the corresponding mode amplitude \(\alpha\) obeys \(\tau  d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha +\beta\). After sample input writes \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is removed, \(\alpha\) decays with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\); as \(\lambda\) approaches 1, recurrent excitation cancels intrinsic leak.

\(\lambda =1\) is the linear condition for an ideal line attractor: any amplitude of that mode persists without input. \(\lambda <1\) produces drift toward baseline, while \(\lambda >1\) produces growth in the linear model and requires nonlinear saturation. Real working memory may tolerate slight leak, correct itself with sensory feedback, or rely on nonlinear discrete attractors; persistent firing does not require connections exactly equal to mathematical 1.

Persistent activity of individual neurons may change over time while a population projection remains stable. Conversely, a condition-averaged cell may look flat because different trial dynamics cancel. Examine decoding across the delay, population trajectories, single-trial drift, and behavioral error together. Short-term memory need not alter synaptic weights online on every trial; the existing recurrent network state can store it.

All modes require stability analysis. One \(\lambda \approx 1\) mode can retain memory, while the remaining eigenvalues should define decaying transverse directions; otherwise noise spreads into irrelevant coordinates. Nonorthogonal eigenvectors can also produce transient amplification. Reporting the longest \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) alone does not establish reliable memory; assess noise accumulation, input selectivity, readout, and reset mechanisms.
keyPoints: The eigenvalue gap \(1-\lambda\) amplifies \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\).
\(\lambda =1\) is the ideal persistence boundary, not a necessary condition for every memory network.
Directions outside the memory mode must also be stable.

derivation.title: Derive the effective time constant from a recurrent eigenvalue
derivation.setup: Project the population equation onto one eigenmode and solve it after input removal.

steps.title: Write the mode equation
steps.explanation: Along an eigenvector, recurrent feedback simply multiplies by \(\lambda\).

steps.title: Remove the input
steps.explanation: After the sample ends, set \(\beta =0\) and combine leak with feedback.

steps.title: Solve the exponential equation
steps.explanation: Initial value \(\alpha _{0}\) decays at rate \((1-\lambda )/\tau\).

steps.title: Read off the time constant
steps.explanation: Write the exponent as \(-t/\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\).

symbolNotes: \(\tau\) and \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) have time units; \(\lambda\) is dimensionless.
\(\alpha\) is a mode amplitude whose units depend on normalization of the firing-rate coordinate.
derivation.unitsCheck: The exponent must be dimensionless, as \((1-\lambda )t/\tau\) is.
derivation.limitCheck: For \(\lambda =0\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau\). As λ→1^-, \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) diverges. When \(\lambda >1\), the formula becomes negative, indicating growth rather than a decay time constant.

workedExample.title: Predict drift during a delay
workedExample.problem: Let \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.99\), and \(\alpha _{0}=10\) after the sample. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and estimate the amplitude after 1 s.
steps: \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.99)=2000 \mathrm{ms}=2 \mathrm{s}\).
After 1 s, \(\alpha =10e^{-1/2}\approx 6.07\).
Although \(\lambda\) is very close to 1, a 1 s delay still loses about 39%, so 'near one' does not mean perfect memory.
workedExample.result: \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=2 \mathrm{s}\), and after 1 s \(\alpha \approx 6.07\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: After one \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=2 \mathrm{s}\), the amplitude should fall to \(e^{-1}\approx 36.8\)% of its initial value.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does increasing \(\lambda\) from 0.99 to 1.01 not simply lengthen memory a little?
selfCheck.answer: It crosses the stability boundary. The linear mode changes from slow decay to exponential growth and needs another nonlinearity to limit amplitude.

pitfalls: Using the \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) formula for \(\lambda >1\) and still calling it a positive decay time constant.
Examining only condition-averaged persistent firing and ignoring single-trial drift.

modules.title: Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage
modules.guidingQuestion: How does random-dot evidence become a choice process with leak, bias, noise, and absorbing bounds?
paragraphs: Random-dot motion provides noisy evidence at every moment. Define \(a>0\) as support for right and \(a<0\) as support for left, and write \(\tau a da/dt=-a+e(t)+\gamma (t)\). The conditional mean of \(e(t)\) varies with signed coherence, while \(\gamma\) is zero-mean noise. The -a term is leak and discounts old evidence; a classic perfect DDM often omits it, whereas this lecture uses the more general leaky accumulator.

The initial condition \(a(0)=b\) represents starting bias; absorbing boundaries \(a=\pm B\) determine first-passage choice and decision time. Positive b puts +B closer, usually making that choice more frequent and faster. Raising B typically increases accuracy and RT; increasing drift magnitude raises accuracy and shortens RT; increasing noise broadens trajectories, changes both, and may create more fast-error trials.

Reaction time also contains nondecision time: sensory encoding and motor execution occur outside accumulator passage. Attributing all RT to evidence accumulation misestimates the bound or drift. Leak, collapsing bounds, urgency, and across-trial variability can produce similar distributions, so constrain parameters with the full choice–RT likelihood and model comparison.

In simulation, update a with a small step \(\Delta t\) and stop at the first boundary crossing; do not average after crossing and then decide. Noise scaling must vary with the square root of \(\Delta t\). Adding a fixed-variance noise term each step makes the model change when the time step changes. Begin numerical self-study with deterministic constant evidence, then add randomness to understand the distribution.
keyPoints: This lecture's accumulator includes leak and must be distinguished from a perfect DDM.
Choice and decision time are determined jointly by the first boundary crossing.
Nondecision time and time-step-dependent noise scaling cannot be omitted.

derivation.title: A leaky accumulator under constant evidence
derivation.setup: Temporarily ignore noise and bounds and solve the trajectory under constant evidence \(\mu\).

steps.title: Write the deterministic equation
steps.explanation: Set \(e(t)=\mu\) and \(\gamma (t)=0\).

steps.title: Find the steady state
steps.explanation: Set the derivative to zero; the equilibrium value equals the constant evidence.

steps.title: Shift the variable
steps.explanation: Let \(z=a-\mu\) to obtain homogeneous decay.

steps.title: Restore the initial condition
steps.explanation: Use \(a(0)=b\) to obtain the full solution.

symbolNotes: a, \(\mu\), and b share the same evidence-state units.
\(\tau a\) is in seconds or milliseconds; B has the same units as a.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(da/dt\) has units of state/time; dividing every state term on the right by \(\tau a\) gives the same units.
derivation.limitCheck: The no-leak limit requires \(\tau a\to \infty\) together with appropriate input scaling. As \(t\to \infty\), \(a\to \mu\); if \(|\mu |<B\), a deterministic trajectory never reaches a boundary.

workedExample.title: Determine a deterministic first-passage time
workedExample.problem: Let \(\tau a=1 \mathrm{s}\), \(b=0\), \(\mu =2\), and \(B=1\). Ignoring noise, find the time to +B.
steps: The solution is \(a(t)=2(1-e^{-t})\).
Taking the natural logarithm gives \(t=\ln 2\approx 0.693 \mathrm{s}\).
workedExample.result: The decision time is about 0.693 s, and the positive boundary is chosen.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The steady state 2 exceeds bound 1, so the trajectory must cross. If \(\mu \le 1\) and \(b=0\), a deterministic leaky trajectory never reaches +B.

selfCheck.prompt: Why do identical coherence values yield different choices and RTs?
selfCheck.answer: Each trial has a different noise path, which changes both the first-passage time and which boundary is reached first.

pitfalls: Treating the leaky equation as a classic no-leak DDM.
Changing \(\Delta t\) in a simulation without rescaling the noise and thereby creating a time-step artifact.

modules.title: Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping
modules.guidingQuestion: Which aspects of an accumulator can behavioral curves and LIP firing constrain, and what can they not prove?
paragraphs: A psychometric function plots P(choice|signed coherence). Choice is nearly uncertain around zero coherence and saturates toward the correct option as coherence magnitude grows. Horizontal displacement suggests bias, while slope reflects overall sensitivity but also depends on sensory noise, integration, and lapses. An accuracy curve alone often cannot distinguish drift, bound, and noise.

A chronometric function plots \(E[RT|coherence]\), typically with slower responses to weak evidence and faster responses to strong evidence. Report correct and error RTs, distribution quantiles, and nondecision time rather than the mean alone. Different models can share a mean curve while differing in tails, fast errors, or conditional accuracy; joint fitting supplies stronger constraints.

During motion decisions, LIP neurons often show choice-selective ramps that approach a similar firing level before response, consistent with accumulation to bound. Yet condition averaging can make step-like single trials appear as a smooth ramp, and urgency or motor plans can also increase over time. Ramping is a neural correlate, not a unique cellular implementation.

Stronger tests map parameter changes to neural predictions: coherence should change ramp slope, prior bias can shift the starting point, and speed instructions can alter bound-like termination. Trial-level neural fluctuations should predict choice and RT. Even if all hold, LIP could read rather than generate the decision variable; temporally precise perturbation and network-wide recording are needed to distinguish these roles.
keyPoints: Psychometric and chronometric functions should be interpreted jointly.
A condition-averaged ramp does not uniquely imply a single-trial ramp.
Quantitative parameter-to-neural-curve predictions are stronger than shape analogy.

workedExample.title: Identify bias from simplified psychometric data
workedExample.problem: At signed coherences -10, 0, and +10%, the probabilities of a right choice are 0.15, 0.65, and 0.93. Does the pattern suggest a rightward bias?
steps: An unbiased model generally predicts about 0.5 at 0 coherence.
The observed 0.65 exceeds 0.5, suggesting a starting-point or choice-rule bias toward the right.
A confidence interval and lapse model are still needed; one proportion cannot identify the source of bias.
workedExample.result: The data suggest a right-choice bias but cannot distinguish initial-state, reward, or motor bias.
workedExample.sanityCheck: At strong evidence on the two sides, probabilities approach 0 and 1 respectively, so the sign convention for direction is consistent.

selfCheck.prompt: Why can mean LIP ramp slopes alone not distinguish accumulation from averaged discrete steps?
selfCheck.answer: Both forms of single-trial dynamics can yield similar smooth curves when different onset or choice times are averaged, requiring single-trial model comparison.

pitfalls: Equating psychometric slope directly with one sensory-noise parameter.
Using resemblance to a ramp-to-threshold plot in place of a causal test.

modules.title: Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries
modules.guidingQuestion: How does a nonlinear recurrent two-population model amplify a weak bias into one of two stable choices?
paragraphs: The reduced Wong–Wang model uses two population variables for recurrent pools supporting the two choices. Self-excitation maintains an activated pool, cross-inhibition suppresses its competitor, and slow synaptic gating supplies an accumulation time scale. Write the dynamics as \(dS_{1}/dt=G_{1}(S_{1},S_{2})\) and \(dS_{2}/dt=G_{2}(S_{1},S_{2})\); the transfer function and parameter values determine the nullcline shapes.

Intersections of \(G_{1}=0\) and \(G_{2}=0\) are fixed points. Under absent or weak evidence, a common topology contains a low-activity undecided state, two choice attractors, and a saddle on the basin boundary. Other parameter settings produce other topologies, so the schematic is not a universal theorem. A separatrix through the saddle assigns initial states and noise paths to the two attractor basins.

Signed evidence makes the two inputs asymmetric, shifts the nullclines, and expands the correct-choice basin. Strong evidence drives trajectories away from the boundary more quickly, usually increasing accuracy and lowering RT; at zero evidence, noise determines the basin. Unlike a DDM with explicit absorbing bounds, choice termination can be defined by entry into an attractor neighborhood, with nonlinear recurrent feedback itself stabilizing the outcome.

Read a phase portrait by inserting test points on both sides of each nullcline to determine arrows and then following trajectories; intersection count alone is insufficient. Keep experimental links at the proper level: the model can generate behavioral curves, population recordings can test competitive dynamics, and perturbing one pool predicts a basin shift. These results show compatibility, not that cortex implements this exact reduced equation.
keyPoints: Nullcline intersections are fixed points; their stability requires a separate test.
A separatrix is the boundary between choice basins.
Evidence biases one attractor by changing input and geometry.

derivation.title: Classify fixed-point stability from the local Jacobian
derivation.setup: Linearize the two-dimensional nonlinear dynamics around any intersection.

steps.title: Define the equilibrium
steps.explanation: At intersection \(S^{*}\), both derivatives are zero.

steps.title: Write a small perturbation
steps.explanation: Let \(\delta S=S-S^{*}\) and retain first-order terms.

steps.title: Write the Jacobian
steps.explanation: Its four partial derivatives describe local self- and cross-feedback.
steps.latex: J=\begin{bmatrix}\partial G_1/\partial S_1&\partial G_1/\partial S_2\\\partial G_2/\partial S_1&\partial G_2/\partial S_2\end{bmatrix}

steps.title: Read the eigenvalues
steps.explanation: The fixed point is locally stable if both eigenvalues have negative real parts; one positive and one negative makes it a saddle.

symbolNotes: S1 and S2 are commonly dimensionless synaptic-gating variables, and Gi has units gating/time.
Jacobian eigenvalues have units 1/time.
derivation.unitsCheck: The derivative \(G_{i}/\partial S_{j}\) has units 1/time, matching a local exponential growth or decay rate.
derivation.limitCheck: Recovery slows as an eigenvalue's real part approaches 0; a positive eigenvalue destabilizes the fixed point.

workedExample.title: Classify two points from their Jacobians
workedExample.problem: Point A has Jacobian eigenvalues -2 and -0.5 s^-1; point B has +1 and -3 s^-1. Classify them.
steps: Both real parts at A are negative, so every small perturbation decays.
At B, one direction grows and the other decays.
A is therefore a local attractor and B a saddle; B's stable manifold can form a separatrix.
workedExample.result: A is stable, and B is a saddle.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The eigenvalue units match the given s^-1; positive and negative signs denote growth and decay, respectively.

selfCheck.prompt: Why do two choice attractors generally require a saddle or basin boundary between them?
selfCheck.answer: Distinct basins of attraction in a continuous dynamical system must be separated by a boundary that flows to neither attractor. In two dimensions, that boundary is commonly the stable manifold of a saddle.

pitfalls: Treating a nullcline itself as a trajectory.
Mapping a reduced-model attractor one-to-one onto a single anatomical population.

objectives: Organize stimulus, action, reward, and synaptic eligibility into a three-factor learning rule, explaining why naive reward-gated Hebbian learning remains excessively strong.
Derive the reward-baseline covariance update and matching equilibrium, stating assumptions such as stationary reward and the choice rule at each step.
Derive Rescorla–Wagner learning from squared prediction error and use blocking to explain why an already predicted reward produces no further learning.
Express delayed reward as a temporal-difference error and distinguish state value, action value, reward-prediction error, and dopamine response.
Read dopamine timelines for early reward, cue transfer, and omission while preserving the evidential boundary for alternatives such as salience.
prerequisiteBridge: The minimal problem in reward learning is not whether reward excites a neuron, but credit assignment: which of many preceding stimuli, actions, and synapses should change because of this outcome?
